Housing & the economy: what the channels said

What 700 videos from 10 channels and groups said about housing, rates, credit, jobs, inflation and markets, how those views changed, which claims hold up, and the cross-market trade ideas that follow.

This report draws on 700 videos from finance and economics channels, with housing as the largest topic. Most videos were uploaded between January and October 2026. (rows 1368, 3302) The mood is bearish. The channel-weighted stance on every topic stayed below zero in every month with enough videos. Most channels describe a frozen housing market, rising credit stress and an energy shock. (rows 1367, 2038, 1821)

Trade ideas

The cross-market ideas in the table below are the report's own analysis. They are not the view of any channel. Each idea starts from evidence the channels gave. It then asks which market has not yet priced that evidence. Two ideas matter most: the credit-stress idea, because distress is moving up the ratings ladder, and the apartment-landlord idea, because it turns the housing freeze into a position.

Key numbers

  • 7.4% — Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate on 15 October 2026 (FRED MORTGAGE30US). MarketWatch, cited by Upside Invest, put it near 7.4% in mid-October 2026. (row 3185)
  • 5.09% — 10-year Treasury yield on 16 October 2026 (FRED DGS10). ITM Trading said yields hit 5.44%, the highest since 2004. The fact-check rates this Partly supported, because the 10-year closed at 5.26% on the upload date. ITM Trading sells the metals it discusses. (row 3253)
  • 8.5 months — new-home months' supply for August 2026 (Census, FRED MSACSR). RE-V cited 9.2 months of builder supply in late August 2026. (row 1621)
  • 4.2% — US unemployment rate for September 2026 (BLS, FRED UNRATE). Eurodollar University cited the official rate at 4.1% in July 2026. It put effective unemployment near 6.2%. (row 2055)

Five findings

  1. Rates above 7% froze the housing market. Existing-home sales fell to 4.09 million a year in June 2026. (row 2087) Upside Invest, citing Redfin, said pending sales in October 2026 were the lowest since 2014, apart from April 2020. (row 3302) The mortgage rate rose from 6.8% in May to 7.2% in mid-September 2026. (rows 1341, 2580) What it implies: Volume, not price, takes the first hit when rates rise.

  2. Prices are flat nationally and split by region. Zillow forecast a 0.1% fall over the next year in June 2026. (row 1338) The NAR median price was $429,000 in May 2026, up 1.3%. (row 1335) RE-V says Austin fell 24.6% from mid-2022 to April 2026, while Wisconsin and North Dakota rose 5.1% in the year to April. (rows 1351, 1355) What it implies: A national average hides local falls and gains.

  3. Builders set the marginal price. RE-V cited 10.3 months of builder supply in May 2026. (row 1329) It says Lennar cut net prices about 25% from the 2022 peak. (row 1333) RE-V says the median new-home price fell below the existing-home price. (row 1774) What it implies: Builder discounts reach resale prices slowly, because existing homes are 85% of sales. (row 1344)

  4. Credit stress moved from private credit toward public credit. Fitch showed a 6.3% private-credit default rate in August 2026. The claim is Partly supported, because most defaults are negotiated amendments. (rows 2038, 2071) Blackstone's BCRED capped payouts at 5% against 10% requested in June 2026. (row 1337) Eurodollar University put triple-C spreads near 1,300 basis points in October 2026. (row 3221) What it implies: Redemption gates and spreads give an earlier signal than the Fitch definition of default.

  5. The Fed hiked while jobs weakened. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points on 16 September 2026. (rows 2177, 2992) Warsh said inflation had run above 2% for 65 months, with PCE at 3.7%. This claim is Supported. (row 1804) Bilyeu's channel cited 29,000 September jobs against 84,000 expected. (row 3082) What it implies: Markets must weigh a hawkish Fed against a hiring slowdown.

How views changed

The stance data are thin. No topic passes the power check, and the largest month-to-month swing is 0.7 points, for inflation. Every topic stayed negative from January to October 2026. Home-price stance moved from -0.5 in January to -1.5 in October, and credit stance from -1.1 to -1.6. Rates stance sat near -1.7 in January, jumped to -0.1 in February, and returned to -1.5 by October. Views on long rates shifted across channels. Eurodollar University said in July 2026 that long rates had a ceiling near 5.1%. (rows 2080, 2075) By September, RE-V and others led with rates above 7% as the cause of the freeze. (rows 2647, 3302)

Trade ideas

These 6 ideas come from reading the 700 videos across markets, not from counting votes. Each one starts from a fact that several channels or the data support, follows it to a market the channels mostly do not discuss, and checks that the price has not already moved. Prices are closes on or before 2026-10-20. This is analysis, not investment advice.

Two candidate rounds (20 bearish-led ideas, then 12 contrarian longs). Each candidate was validated against live prices, valuations, option chains and FRED, then argued against by a separate reviewer. 15 of 32 were killed; these are the six highest-scoring survivors (red-team scores 5-6 of 10), with overlapping ideas merged.

1. Credit stress climbs the ratings ladder

Distress that started in private credit and CCC bonds is now widening BB and single-B spreads, but the broad high-yield index is still near the low end of its range.

The chain. Private-credit and AI-debt stress (rows 3221, 3204) → CCC spreads past 1,300bp → BB and single-B spreads start to widen → High-yield index spread moves from 3.3 toward 4 → HYG falls

Evidence. Eurodollar University reported CCC spreads near 1,300bp on 14 October 2026, above the March 2023 banking-crisis highs (row 3221), and on 1 October that investment-grade spreads had begun to widen with junk (row 2969). The same channel tied the AI boom to debt-financed spending (row 3204). ITM Trading noted junk-bond ETFs down for the year while stocks rose (row 3256). FRED confirms the move: the ICE BofA CCC spread was 13.10 points on 19 October, the high-yield index spread rose from 2.68 to 3.29 in a month, BB from 1.57 to 1.96 and single-B from 2.78 to 3.23. Private-credit default rates (Fitch 6.3%) are not high-yield bond defaults and are not used here.

Why it is not priced. The market has noticed: HYG is at its 52-week low ($76.93, 81.28 high). It has not priced a recession-type move. At 3.29 the index spread sits inside its own 12-month range of 2.60-3.46 while CCC is in distress territory, and investment-grade (0.84) has barely moved. The CCC/HY ratio of about 4x says the market is isolating the weakest names, so the trade is continuation, not an unnoticed gap.

Expression.

  • Primary (options): HYG Mar-2027 75/72 put spread: buy 75 put (mid 1.07, IV 10.3%, open interest 43,318), sell 72 put (mid 0.665, IV 13.7%). Net debit about $0.405, max gain $2.595, breakeven $74.60 (chain 20 Oct 2026). Enter in two tranches, the second after ARCC's 27 Oct results or if the index spread tightens back toward 3.10.
  • Cash alternative: Short HYG, long IEF, weighted by duration so the position is the spread, not the rate level. A cash short pays HYG's ~6% distribution, which is why the put spread is preferred.
  • Add-ons: Optional small ARCC Mar-2027 17/15 put spread (about $0.375), only if ARCC's 27 Oct results show non-accruals at 3% of cost or more. A KRE Mar-2027 70/60 put spread (about $2.60, IV ~23%) as a cheap tail hedge: bank CRE delinquencies are falling, so it is insurance, not a view.

Catalysts. FOMC 28 Oct 2026; ARCC Q3 results 27 Oct and OBDC 4 Nov; October payrolls 6 Nov; Nvidia results 17 Nov (Yahoo; a video gave 18 Nov).

Invalidation. Exit if the ICE BofA high-yield spread (FRED BAMLH0A0HYM2) closes below 2.90, which erases the October move, or the CCC spread (BAMLH0A3HYC) closes below 11.0. First target is an index spread of 3.8-4.0; 4.5 would be a recession print.

Against it. Spread decompression without index contagion may be the regime, not an anomaly. All-in high-yield yields near 8% draw in buyers, and bearish HYG positioning has been squeezed hard before. Shorting private credit is one of the most crowded hedge-fund trades of 2026, which is why the cleaner, liquid index is used instead of BDCs.

Entry snapshot: HYG 76.93 (2026-10-20).

2. The housing freeze keeps renters renting

At 7%+ mortgage rates the channels' own housing evidence (collapsed purchase demand, record prices) is a reason to own apartment landlords, not avoid them, and the best one is priced near its low.

The chain. Mortgage rates above 7% and record prices (row 2589) → Purchase applications collapse (rows 2098, 3083) → Renters cannot buy, so they renew → Low turnover and firmer renewals at Sunbelt apartment REITs → MAA re-rates against REITs as a whole

Evidence. RE-V reported purchase applications down about 55% from the pandemic peak in September 2026 (row 2098), and Felix & Friends said applications hit their lowest since 1995 (row 3083). Upside Invest reported a record $429,000 median price with mortgage rates above 7% (row 2589). Freddie Mac's 30-year rate was 7.40% on 15 October (FRED MORTGAGE30US). MAA's own Q2 2026 data shows the effect: turnover 39.6%, only 10.9% of move-outs leaving to buy a home, renewals +5.2%, occupancy 95.4%. Multifamily starts are down 26% year on year, which shrinks future supply; a video put the supply crossover at late 2027 or early 2028 (row 1372).

Why it is not priced. MAA is at $117.52, 3% above its 52-week low of $113.95, yields 5.3%, has a Hold consensus and 4% short interest. It has lagged VNQ by about 11 points over 12 months even though blended lease growth turned up 100bp in Q2. This is not a crowded long.

Expression.

  • Primary (pair): Long MAA, short VNQ, 1:1 dollars. The pair's sensitivity to the 10-year is close to zero (measured beta to IEF 0.08), so it isolates apartments from rates, and the long side earns about 1.5 points a year more yield. Put on half now; add the second half only if MAA's 28 Oct results hold Q2's +0.7% blended lease growth and 95.3%+ occupancy.
  • Options: MAA Mar-2027 120/125 call spread (sell 125, not the thin 130). The 120 call was 5.0/5.6 on 20 Oct (open interest 282).
  • Add-on: Camden (CPT) after its 5 Nov results, at 2:1 MAA:CPT.

Catalysts. MAA Q3 results 28 Oct 2026; CPT Q3 results 5 Nov; MAA 2027 guidance, early Feb 2027 (the main test).

Invalidation. Exit if MAA's Q3 blended lease growth is below 0% or occupancy below 95.0%, if MAA closes below $113.95, if the initial 2027 same-store revenue guide midpoint is below 0%, or if the MAA/VNQ ratio closes 8% below entry.

Against it. The 'supply crossover, recovery in 2027' story is the industry's own and it keeps slipping: MAA cut its same-store NOI guide to -1.7% to -0.1% in Q2, new leases were -5.3%, and national rental vacancy is still rising (7.3%, FRED RRVRUSQ156N).

Entry snapshot: MAA 117.52 (2026-10-20); VNQ 92.365 (2026-10-20).

3. Title insurance earns through the freeze, but is sold with an annuity book

Fidelity National Financial's title business is earning record margins on depressed volumes; the 20% fall in the stock is the market pricing credit risk in its F&G annuity subsidiary, not title.

The chain. Home sales stuck near 4m (rows 2419, 2043) → Title volumes depressed but stable → FNF title margins at records → F&G private-credit fears drag FNF down → FNF re-rates once F&G's marks are known

Evidence. RE-V reported 3.93 million existing-home sales in August 2026, the second-worst August in 30 years (row 2419), and Eurodollar University reported sales below 4 million (row 2043). Low but steady is the point: FRED shows 3.99 million in September, -2.2% year on year. FNF's title segment earned $448m adjusted pre-tax in Q2 2026, +33% year on year, at a 17.8% margin. F&G is -31% over three months at 0.58x book on private-credit fears.

Why it is not priced. FNF is $40.52, -19% over three months, 7% above its 52-week low of $37.88, at 7.5x forward earnings with a 5.2% dividend. Its fall tracks F&G's, not title: First American, the pure title peer, is a Strong Buy at 9.2x. The market is selling the title franchise along with the annuity book.

Expression.

  • Primary: Long FNF, entered only after BOTH First American's results (21 Oct) and FNF/F&G's (5 Nov). If F&G shows no impairments or book-value hit, hold FNF outright. If it does, hedge with short F&G at 0.35-0.40 FG dollars per FNF dollar (measured beta 0.38).
  • Note: No options expression: the FNF and FG chains are too thin.

Catalysts. First American Q3 results 21 Oct 2026 (title read-through); FNF and F&G Q3 results 5 Nov; NAR existing-home sales for October, 12 Nov.

Invalidation. Exit if FNF's Q3 adjusted title pre-tax margin is below the year-ago level, if F&G reports credit impairments that cut FNF's book value, if FNF closes below $37.88, or if existing-home sales fall below 3.8m SAAR.

Against it. Q2 is the seasonal high, and mortgage rates rose 97bp from 2 July to 15 October, which squeezes refinance orders into Q4 and Q1. Record margins on depressed volumes are more often a peak than a floor, and F&G missed Q4 EPS by 24%.

Entry snapshot: FNF 40.515 (2026-10-20).

4. Gasoline crowds out discretionary spending

Headline retail sales look strong because of gasoline; underneath, discretionary spending has stalled while savings are drawn down, and retail stocks have rallied as if the headline were the story.

The chain. Oil shock lifts gasoline spending (WTI about $102) → Consumers cut extras (rows 3425, 2855) → Saving rate falls, card debt cut (rows 2912, 3142) → Control-group sales stall → Discretionary retailers (XRT) fall back

Evidence. Eurodollar University cited convenience stores reporting cuts to snacks and drinks while gasoline purchases held up (row 3425), and Pepsi's CEO pointing to gas prices as a constraint (row 2855). The same channel reported August spending financed by drawing down savings (row 2912) and a $4.8bn cut in revolving credit (row 3142); FRED confirms the saving rate fell to 4.1% in August from 5.1% in March. September retail sales rose 0.8%, but excluding gasoline only 0.2%, and the control group 0.1% against 0.3% expected (AP, First Trust). All five cited rows come from one channel, so the official data carries this idea.

Why it is not priced. XRT is $87.66, up about 7% in a month and near its 52-week high of $93.52. The market is following the headline sales number, not the gasoline-adjusted one.

Expression.

  • Primary (options): XRT Jan-2027 85/78 put spread: buy 85 put (mid 2.915, open interest 29,258), sell 78 put (mid 1.055). Net debit about $1.86, max gain $5.14, breakeven $83.14, about 2.8:1 (chain 20 Oct 2026). Covers Black Friday, the Walmart and Target results, and November and December retail sales. Take half profit at XRT $81 or below before WMT/TGT.
  • Cash alternative: Short XRT, long IWM, 1:1 beta. Not XLP, which has already rallied about 9% in October.

Catalysts. October retail sales 17 Nov 2026; Target results 18 Nov; Walmart results 19 Nov; Black Friday 27 Nov.

Invalidation. Close if October control-group retail sales (17 Nov) are +0.4% m/m or more with September not revised down, if XRT closes above $93.52, or if the September saving rate prints above 4.6%.

Against it. Holiday forecasts are not weak: the NRF expects +4.2% and Deloitte +4.0-4.8%. September's headline beat by a wide margin and August was revised up to +1.3%. XRT is also a chronically crowded short, which is why only options are used.

Entry snapshot: XRT 87.66 (2026-10-20).

5. When the Fed stops, the front end rallies first

The Fed hiked into a labor market that then printed +29,000 jobs; the 2-year still prices more tightening than a pausing Fed would deliver, while the long end stays weighed down by supply.

The chain. Fed hikes 25bp on 16 Sep (DFEDTARU 3.75 → 4.00) → September payrolls +29,000 (row 3082) → Fed holds on 28 Oct or 9 Dec → 2-year falls toward the 3.88% effective funds rate → 2s10s steepens; Treasuries rebound

Evidence. Tom Bilyeu reported September payrolls of 29,000 against 84,000 expected (row 3082). Eurodollar University reported the 2-year falling 18bp to 4.72% after hot CPI and PPI (row 3303) and the August cut in revolving credit (row 3142). FRED: the Fed's upper bound rose from 3.75 to 4.00 on 17 September; the effective rate is 3.88%; the 2-year was 4.74% and the 10-year 5.09% on 16 October. The 10-year's closing high was 5.31% on 5 October.

Why it is not priced. The 2-year at 4.74% sits about 86bp above the effective funds rate, so the front end still prices more hikes. The rally has started (2-year 4.89% on 29 Sep → 4.74%), but the curve steepening so far came from long yields rising, not short yields falling.

Expression.

  • Primary (futures): A DV01-neutral 2s10s steepener: long 2-year Treasury futures (ZT), short 10-year (ZN). Half size until after the 28 Oct FOMC; add only if the Fed holds. If only the 'Fed is done' view is wanted, long Mar-27/Jun-27 SOFR futures instead.
  • Options (duration): TLT Mar-2027 82/88 call spread: buy 82 call (1.94/1.97), sell 88 call (0.62/0.64), open interest above 10,000 on both. Net about $1.325, max gain $4.675, breakeven $83.33 with TLT at $80.07; IV about 14%. Size it small: big investors already moved into bonds in October (BofA survey), so this leg is a hedge, not a contrarian bet. Do not add before the November refunding.
  • ETF fallback: SHY long / TLT short at about 8.3:1 notional for DV01 neutrality (this is a 2s/20s trade, not 2s10s).

Catalysts. FOMC 28 Oct 2026; October payrolls 6 Nov; Treasury quarterly refunding, early Nov (date not confirmed); FOMC and dot plot 9 Dec.

Invalidation. Exit if the Fed hikes on 28 Oct or 9 Dec, if 2s10s (FRED T10Y2Y) closes below 0.20, if the 2-year closes above 4.95%, or (TLT leg) if the 10-year closes above 5.31% or the 30-year above 5.60%.

Against it. Inflation, not jobs, is driving the Fed: September CPI was 3.7% against 3.6% expected, and October-hike odds jumped from 22% to 41.5% on 14 October. After the September hike the curve flattened from 0.33 to 0.20 within three sessions, which is exactly the move that kills this trade. Prediction markets price a December hike at 76%.

Entry snapshot: TLT 80.07 (2026-10-20); SHY 81.33 (2026-10-20).

6. Mortgage REITs: own the servicing hedge, not the premium

Frozen refinancing makes mortgage servicing rights more valuable. Annaly owns a large servicing book and trades below book; AGNC owns none and trades at a premium to a freshly cut book. The pair has not separated them.

The chain. Sub-3% mortgages locked in, refinancing frozen (row 2098) → Mortgage applications at 1995 lows (row 3083) → Servicing rights gain value when prepayments stall → Annaly's servicing book offsets agency-bond losses → NLY outperforms AGNC

Evidence. RE-V reported purchase applications down about 55% from peak (row 2098) and Felix & Friends reported applications at their lowest since 1995 (row 3083). The servicing link is this report's inference; no video names either REIT. Company data: AGNC's tangible book fell 16.9% in Q3 to $7.13 (filed 19 Oct). Annaly's servicing book was $4.1bn, 21% of its capital, at Q2.

Why it is not priced. AGNC trades at 1.24x its new tangible book ($8.84/$7.13); NLY at 0.91x its June book ($18.27/$20.15). The NLY/AGNC price ratio is 2.068, inside its one-year range of 1.987-2.187, so the market has not yet split them.

Expression.

  • Conditional pair: Long NLY, short AGNC, $0.86 of AGNC per $1 of NLY (beta-weighted). Enter at the 21 Oct open ONLY if Annaly's Q3 book (reported after the 20 Oct close) is at least $18.14 (a fall of 10% or less), NLY trades at or below 1.05x it, and AGNC is still at or above 1.15x its $7.13 book. Check the AGNC borrow fee is under ~1% first.
  • Book note: The pair gains when rates rise, so it partly offsets the 'Fed stops' idea above. Net the two if both are held.

Catalysts. Annaly Q3 results after the close, 20 Oct 2026; FOMC 28 Oct; AGNC ex-dividend 29 Oct (the short pays).

Invalidation. Do not enter if Annaly's Q3 book is $16.74 or lower (a fall matching AGNC's). After entry, exit if the NLY/AGNC ratio closes below 1.987, if NLY's price/book reaches AGNC's, or if the high-yield spread passes 3.75%.

Against it. NLY's discount uses a stale June book; if its Q3 book fell 9-10%, the gap is already priced and a good print could be 'sell the news'. NLY also carries residential credit risk, and credit spreads have widened 45bp since late September. On 20 Oct AGNC rose 4.9% against NLY's 3.0%.

Entry snapshot: NLY 18.27 (2026-10-20); AGNC 8.84 (2026-10-20).

Addendum: ideas checked and rejected

22 other candidates went through the same checks. Most bearish ones failed for one reason: the market had already priced the bad news. They are listed so the reader can see what the market already knows.

Folded into the six ideas: BDC dividend cuts (c08) and the regional-bank tail hedge (c20) became add-ons to idea 1; long Treasuries (d10) became the TLT leg of idea 5.

Method: candidates were generated from the signal ledger (see Method & limits), then each was checked against live prices, valuations and option chains, and argued against by a separate reviewer before selection. Conviction is the reviewers' judgement, not a probability. ITM Trading is a precious-metals dealer.

Full report

Housing

Prices: a stall, a regional split, and a dispute over the word "crash"

RE-V (the ReVenture channel) leads the housing coverage. It argues that US home prices are falling in many metros and that a larger correction is coming. The channel cites its own ReVenture app and its own overvaluation index. It says the US market was about 13% overvalued in February 2026. (row 1368)

Zillow supplies the main outside forecasts. RE-V reports that Zillow cut its 2026 price forecast from 1.9% to 0.5% in March 2026. (row 1358) By May 2026 the Zillow figure was 0.3%. (row 1349) In June 2026 Zillow forecast a 0.1% fall over the next year. It showed 27 of the top 50 metros with negative forecasts. (row 1338) RE-V says ReVenture's metro forecasts were about four times more accurate than Zillow's from February 2025 to 2026. That accuracy claim comes from ReVenture itself. (rows 1349, 1338)

The national price data are mixed. Realtor.com reported median list prices down 2.5% year on year in July 2026. (row 1326) The same video says Redfin showed record median sale prices. RE-V explains the gap by luxury homes selling while cheaper homes stay unsold. (row 1326) Upside Invest reported a record median price of $429,000 in August 2026. (row 2589) The NAR median for May 2026 was also $429,000, up 1.3% year on year. (row 1335) Sales of homes above $1 million rose 4% year on year in the Upside Invest report. Sales below $250,000 fell 10%. (row 2589)

Eurodollar University reported in July 2026 that both Case-Shiller and FHFA measures showed prices flattening or slipping. (row 2087) RE-V cited Case-Shiller growth of only 0.7% year on year for March 2026. (row 1339)

The channels disagree on regions. RE-V says supply in the South and West is back to pre-pandemic levels. It says the Northeast and Midwest remain about 50% short. (row 1355) It reports Austin down about 24% from June 2022 to January 2026, on Zillow data. (row 1364) It also reports rising prices in Milwaukee (+5.2% in September 2026) and Alaska (+5.8%). (rows 1643, 1914) New Jersey home values rose 3.3% in the year to July 2026. (row 1321) San Francisco values rose almost 10% in August 2026. (row 1572)

Some channels dispute the "crash" story. Tom Bilyeu says in September 2026 that US homeownership is about 65%, as it was in the 1970s. He says this undercuts the claim that affordability has worsened across the board. (row 2621) Doomberg, in a submitted video from September 2026, argues that homeowners hold large equity. He says this makes the market different from 2008. (row 2539)

Sales, inventory and demand

Almost every channel agrees that sales volume is very low. RE-V reported annualised existing-home sales of 3.9 million in January 2026. It called this the lowest on record. (row 1367) NAR reported 3.98 million for March 2026. (row 1351) Sales rose to 4.17 million in May 2026. (row 1335) Sales then fell to 4.09 million in June. (row 2087) Eurodollar University said sales fell below 4 million in August 2026. (row 2043) ABC News, as cited by RE-V, put August sales at 3.93 million. (row 2419)

RE-V says only 4.7% of homes changed hands in a year during 2023-2025. The normal figure is 6.1%. (row 1367) It says ReVenture's buyer demand index read 9 out of 100 in March 2026. (row 1361) It read 10 in July 2026. (row 1326)

Redfin supplies the one counter-signal in the spring. RE-V reported Redfin pending sales at their highest since September 2022 in May 2026, up 7.7% year on year. (row 1346) The same video says NAR pending sales stayed about 30% below the long-term average. (row 1346) The autumn data were weaker. Upside Invest, citing Redfin, said pending sales in October 2026 were the lowest since 2014, apart from April 2020. (row 3302) It said 14.5% of deals signed in September 2026 were cancelled. (row 3302) RE-V had cited a 14% cancellation rate for February 2026. (row 1357)

Inventory is the main dispute. RE-V said in February 2026 that about 900,000 homes were listed, the most since December 2019. It concluded that the shortage was over. (row 1368) NAR figures cited by Eurodollar University showed 1.62 million existing homes for sale in August 2026. That is 4.9 months of supply, the most since November 2019. (row 2043) RE-V says Tennessee had 37,000 listings in September 2026. (row 2098) It says Seattle had 12,000. (row 1786) Redfin, cited by Upside Invest, said sales fell in all 50 of the largest metros in September 2026. (row 3302)

Builders: the price war

RE-V argues that builders drive the price correction. It says the median new-home price fell from $460,000 in October 2022 to $394,000 in July 2026. It says this is below the $434,000 existing-home price, for the first time since the late 1990s. (row 1774) Earlier in 2026 RE-V used Census figures of $392,000 against $410,000. (row 1366) A submitted video from October 2026 says new homes are cheaper than old ones in some markets. The gap runs from $25,000 to $55,000 or more. (row 3154)

Builder inventory is the central figure. RE-V cited Census data showing 9.7 months of builder supply in March 2026. (row 1359) It cited 10.3 months for May 2026. (row 1329) It cited 9.2 months in late August. (row 1621) RE-V says only recession periods saw such levels before. (row 1774)

Lennar is the main case study. RE-V says Lennar cut net prices about 25% from the 2022 peak. (rows 1333, 1319) D.R. Horton cut about 12%. Its cancellation rate rose to 20% from 17%. (rows 1774, 1319) A submitted video from October 2026 cites Hunterbrook's report that Milrose entities bought more than 700 Lennar homes. These purchases came in roughly a month. They raise questions about reported deliveries. (row 3168) That video also says Lennar's average selling price was $372,000 and incentives were about 12%. (row 3168)

RE-V says builder cuts reach resale prices slowly. Existing homes are 85% of annual sales. (row 1344) The NAHB chief economist expects resale prices to falter, according to RE-V. (row 1344) Felix & Friends relayed JPMorgan's view in April 2026 that builders do well in a bullish scenario. (row 2302)

Mortgages, rates and lock-in

Mortgage rates shaped the argument in the second half of 2026. In February 2026 RE-V credited a $200 billion Fannie Mae bond-buying order with a fall from about 6.2% to 6.05%. (row 1368) Patrick Boyle described the same order in January 2026 as an attempt to cut rates by decree. (row 1836) RE-V reported 6.7% in March 2026. (row 1358) It reported 6.8% in May. (row 1341) Rates then rose sharply. Upside Invest reported 7.2% in mid-September 2026. (row 2580) Felix & Friends reported 7.45% in late September. (row 2894) Upside Invest reported nearly 7.3% in early October. (row 3012) MarketWatch, cited by Upside Invest, put the figure near 7.4% in mid-October. (row 3185)

The channels link this rise to the 10-year Treasury yield. Boyle calls that yield the wholesale price of money behind mortgages. (row 1804) The Fed record supports a rate-pressure backdrop. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at Jackson Hole that inflation had run above 2% for 65 months, with PCE at 3.7%. This claim is rated Supported. (row 1804)

Lock-in is the second theme. RE-V says 22% of mortgages carry a rate of 6% or more. It says 19% carry less than 3%, citing Fannie Mae's database. (row 1332) JPMorgan, cited by RE-V, says about 30% of owners have rates above 5.5%. (row 1325) California is an exception: 28% hold sub-3% loans. (row 1350) Bilyeu argues in September 2026 that sub-3% owners refuse to sell. (row 2647)

Eurodollar University changed its view. In July 2026 it said long rates hit a ceiling near 5.1%, because higher rates would collapse housing. (rows 2080, 2075) By October 2026 other channels reported rates above 7%. Eurodollar University also argues that weak jobs and income, not rates, hold back demand. (row 2066)

Distress and credit

RE-V places most distress in Florida. It cited 118,000 US foreclosure filings in the first quarter of 2026, up 26% year on year. Florida rose 44%. (row 1353) It reported mortgage delinquency of 4.4% in Q1 2026 from the Mortgage Bankers Association. (row 1322) RE-V cites FHA delinquency of 11.88% in Q1 2026. (row 1319) It cites ICE figures of 5-6% seriously delinquent for FHA loans. (row 1382) These two FHA figures use different measures. RE-V also notes the overall serious delinquency rate of 1% is far below the 5% of 2009-2010. (row 1382)

United Wholesale Mortgage added a lender signal in August 2026. Eurodollar University reported a loss and a dividend suspension. (row 2066) RE-V reported a $452 million quarterly loss and a 49% share drop. (row 1406)

Private credit links housing to finance. Blackstone arranged a secondary sale for a US real estate fund of about $11 billion in September 2026. (rows 2038, 2039) Fitch default data show records in mid-2026. This claim is rated Partly supported. Most of these "defaults" are negotiated amendments and extensions, and the index began only in August 2024. (rows 2038, 2040)

Rents

RE-V argues that rents have turned. BLS rent inflation was 2.6% year on year in April 2026, down from 9% after the pandemic. (row 1354) CoreLogic put single-family asking-rent growth at 1.3% to start 2026. (row 1354) Zillow's single-family rent index was up 2.7% in May 2026. (row 1341) Austin typical rent fell from $1,650 in 2022 to $1,250 in 2026. (row 1380) Cape Coral rents fell 11% year on year in August 2026, per RealPage. (row 1484)

Not every market follows. San Francisco rents rose 11% year on year in June 2026. (row 1336) Chicago ranked first for four-year rent growth. (row 1386) Patrick Boyle argues in May 2026 that shelter costs rose 3% and that CPI lags new-lease rents. (row 1821) A Peak Prosperity video from July 2026 argues that BLS owner's equivalent rent misses taxes and insurance. (row 3359)

RE-V reports a buy-versus-rent gap of $761 a month in May 2026. (row 1346) Dowd, in a submitted video from August 2026, argues that falling tenant rents lead home prices down. He ties the decline to border closure. (row 1596)

Commercial real estate

The Timeless Investor, run by an operator who says he buys apartment buildings, supplies most of the commercial real estate argument. (rows 2688, 2699) The channel argues in January 2026 that 2021-2022 loans at 3% or less must refinance at 6-8%. (row 2714) It cites $1.5 trillion maturing from late 2025 through 2027. (row 2709) Other maturity figures include $957 billion in 2026 (row 2703) and $940 billion for 2024-2026. (row 2697) These totals differ by period and source.

The channel reports office CMBS delinquency of 11.76% and vacancy of 19.4%. (row 2714) It reports multifamily delinquency of 1.37% in Q3 2025. (row 2697) RE-V reports that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac multifamily defaults hit their highest since 2009-2010. (row 1324) A submitted video from July 2026 says good properties trade at 80 cents on the dollar. It expects supply and absorption to cross in late 2027 or early 2028. (row 1372) Peak Prosperity said in October 2026 that a San Francisco tower drew zero bids. (row 3361)

The Timeless Investor argues that Portland's supply collapsed. Permits fell from 4,112 in 2022 to below 700 by 2025. (row 2700) It cites Moody's CPPI at about 20% below the July 2022 peak. (row 2699)

First-time buyers and affordability

Several channels cite NAR's survey, which puts the median first-time buyer age at 40. (rows 1845, 2202, 2200) The claim is rated Supported. The Mortgage Bankers Association argues that mortgage records show a typical age near 32. (rows 1372, 2202) Bilyeu says first-timers are 21% of the market, the lowest share recorded. (row 2200) Bilyeu says homes cost 2 times income in 1970 and about 5 times now. (row 2216)

RE-V puts the payment burden at 38% of income in May 2026. It says 27% is the long-term median. (row 1349) Eurodollar University says the income needed for a starter home rose from about $43,000 in 2019 to about $78,000. (row 2055)

ITM Trading is a precious-metals dealer. It sells the metals it discusses. Its guests describe a housing crash of 40-60% (row 3272) and an energy shock (row 3258). A speaker on another ITM video alleges appraisal fraud in Texas. (row 3289)

How the argument changed

In January 2026 the case rested on commercial debt and Portland's supply collapse. (rows 2714, 2700) From February to May 2026 RE-V focused on falling prices and record-low sales. (rows 1366, 1351) In June and July the focus moved to builder inventory and Florida losses. (rows 1329, 1332) From September 2026 rates above 7% became the lead explanation for a frozen market. (rows 2647, 3302)

What to watch

  • Mortgage rates and the 10-year yield, which channels call the main driver. (rows 1804, 2894)
  • Pending home sales and cancellation rates: NAR and Redfin. (rows 3302, 1357)
  • Builder months of supply from the Census Bureau. (row 1621)
  • Inventory against normal levels, by state. (rows 1355, 2043)
  • Foreclosure filings and FHA delinquency. (rows 1353, 1382)
  • Zillow and ReVenture price forecasts, and median list prices. (rows 1338, 1326)
  • Rent indices from RealPage, BLS and Zillow. (rows 1354, 1341)
  • Commercial real estate maturities and office delinquency. (rows 2714, 2709)
  • The share of mortgages at 6% or more against those below 3%. (rows 1332, 2098)

Rates and the Fed

From cuts to hikes at the Fed

In February 2026, RE-V said the Fed cut rates seven times from August 2024. Rates fell from 5.5% to 3.7%. (row 1367) RE-V argued that buyer demand still fell. (row 1367) In March 2026, Felix & Friends said the dot plot showed one cut for 2026, down from two. (row 2306) In April 2026, RE-V cited the FedWatch tool. It showed a 58% chance of no cut by September and a 17% chance of a hike. (row 1354)

Kevin Warsh took over as chair in mid-2026. In June, Felix & Friends said he would not take orders from the White House and distrusted forward guidance. (row 2268) In July, the FOMC held rates at 3.25-3.5% on a 9-3 vote. Three dissenters wanted a hike. (row 2073) At Jackson Hole, Warsh said inflation had run above 2% for 65 months, with PCE at 3.7%. Fact-check: Supported. (row 1804) Upside Invest said markets then priced a 66% chance of a September hike. (row 2614)

The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points on 16 September 2026. The new range was 3.75-4%. (rows 2177, 2992) Peak Prosperity gave 3.5-3.75% as the old range. This conflicts with the July figure. (rows 3325, 2073) In October, Upside Invest said markets priced a nearly 80% chance of a pause. Most officials still expected another hike by December. (row 3220)

The Fed also expects inflation above 2% until 2029. Fact-check: Supported. The AI link comes only from the meeting minutes, which cite tariffs and energy costs first. (row 3113) Upside Invest argued in October that AI spending feeds inflation and keeps the Fed hawkish. (row 3113)

Is the curve warning of inflation or of a policy error?

Eurodollar University gives the most distinct reading. It argues the flat curve shows Fed policy risk, not inflation risk. The 2-10 spread was 30 basis points in July and 20 basis points in September 2026. (rows 2073, 2532) It compares 2026 with 2008 and 2018. In both years, it says, markets priced hikes that later reversed. (rows 2069, 2733) In July it noted TIPS break-evens barely moved as oil rose. (row 2075)

Other channels reject that view. Peak Prosperity argues in October 2026 that the Fed will choose to print money and weaken the dollar. (row 3320) ITM Trading and Felix & Friends call the Fed's $40 billion monthly reserve purchases quantitative easing. (rows 3282, 2312) ITM Trading's guest Axel Merk says Warsh opposes QE. (row 3250) Upside Invest cites Mark Zandi, who calls a hike a policy error. (row 2580)

Long yields: vigilantes or normalisation

The 30-year yield crossed 5% at a 13 May 2026 auction, the first time since 2007. (row 2222) Bilyeu noted that long yields rose almost one point after six cuts totalling 175 basis points. (row 2222) Boyle cited HSBC, which calls this the "danger zone". Bank of America found that 62% of fund managers expect 6%. (row 1817)

The peak came later. The 30-year reached 5.33% on 20 August 2026. (row 2670) The 10-year hit 5.23% in late September and 5.34% in early October. (rows 2732, 3012) Peak Prosperity said the 30-year touched 5.7% on 7 October. (row 3316) ITM Trading said Treasury yields reached 5.44%, the highest since 2004. Fact-check: Partly supported. The 10-year closed at 5.26% on the upload date and never passed 5.31%. (row 3253) Eurodollar University said the 10-year fell to 5.08% after hot CPI data in mid-October. (row 3303)

Eurodollar University argues the story is curve normalisation, not a buyer strike. It says the 30-year is only about 20-25 basis points above its October 2023 level. (rows 2060, 2050) It cites New York Fed term premiums, which stayed flat. (row 2056) Bilyeu, Felix & Friends and Peak Prosperity disagree. They say the bond market no longer trusts government spending. (rows 2183, 3337)

Channels name different drivers. Peak Prosperity ties the 10-year to oil, up from 4.2% before the Iran war to 4.7-4.8% in September 2026. (row 3333) Eurodollar University said in July that this link had broken. By September it said oil was reconnecting to the 2-year yield. (rows 2080, 2171) Japan is the other focus. Felix & Friends said Japan sold $66 billion of Treasuries in one month. (row 2247) Upside Invest cited Brad Setser, who says China may hold Treasuries through custodians in Canada and Belgium. (row 3544)

Debt, deficits and the exit routes

US debt passed $40 trillion in August 2026. (rows 2059, 2670) The channels disagree on interest costs. The Timeless Investor cited $931 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026. (row 2670) Bilyeu and Upside Invest cited $1.4 trillion and $1 trillion. (rows 2183, 3544) The Timeless Investor cited a 6.3% deficit for fiscal 2025. (row 2682) Boyle expected over 7% for 2026. (row 1821) Peak Prosperity says debt grew $3.5 trillion in 12 months against a $1.9 trillion stated deficit. (row 3351)

Debt held by the public stood near 101% of GDP in 2026. The CBO projects 120% by 2036. (row 1817) Fact-check: Partly supported. The claim of 100% in 2024 and 120% by the early 2030s broadly holds. (row 2682) Felix & Friends and Bilyeu give 120-122%. (rows 2247, 2891)

Channels expect different exits. In April 2026, Felix & Friends argued the US would drift toward financial repression. (row 2294) In August, the Treasury doubled buybacks from $2 billion to $4 billion. (row 2670) ITM Trading said yield curve control was coming. (row 3277) Peak Prosperity called the buybacks yield curve control. (row 3339) The Timeless Investor noted the $28 billion programme covers 0.14% of long paper. (row 2670) In October, Felix & Friends said repression is impossible. The 10-year yield exceeds inflation. (row 2987)

Gold and the dealer's interest

ITM Trading sells the metals it discusses. Its guests say central banks hold more gold than Treasuries. (rows 3279, 3283) Felix & Friends also says central banks are buying gold at record pace. Fact-check: Partly supported. Q2 2026 buying of 289 tonnes set a second-quarter record. (rows 2204, 2227, 2228, 2230) Goldman Sachs forecast gold at $4,900 by end-2026. Fact-check: Supported. Goldman cut it to $4,650 on 23 September 2026 as Fed hikes weighed. (rows 2229, 2236, 2248)

Mortgages

RE-V put the 30-year mortgage rate at 6.74% in August 2026. (row 1485) Upside Invest said 7% in September. (row 2592) Submitted directly, one video put it at 7.5% in October. (row 2979)

What to watch

Credit and banking

Private credit: size, defaults and gates

The channels agree that private credit is the weak point in US lending. They disagree on its size and on how bad the losses are.

Felix & Friends said in February 2026 that the market grew from $500 billion to $3 trillion. (row 2322) In March 2026 Felix & Friends cited Moody's for a market above $2 trillion and a path to $4 trillion in three years. (row 2311) That Moody's claim is Partly supported. Patrick Boyle put the market at $1.8 trillion in March 2026. (row 1827)

Boyle argued in March 2026 that private credit hides losses. Funds advertise loss rates below 0.1%. Public speculative-grade debt defaults at 4.5%. (row 1827) He cited a Goldman Sachs study. Of 150 European credit events since 2017, 146 were quiet handovers. (row 1827)

Eurodollar University and a submitted video then tracked the Fitch default rate through 2026. Fitch showed a trailing 12-month rate of 6.3% in August, across about 1,300 US borrowers. (rows 2038, 2039) The Fitch claim is Partly supported. The rate rose to successive records in mid-2026, and the Financial Times reported troubled loans at the 20 largest listed funds at their highest since 2017. (rows 1805, 2185) But Fitch's "defaults" are mostly negotiated amendments, such as PIK switches and extensions. The index began only in August 2024. (rows 2038, 2071) Stressed maturity extensions caused 45% of August defaults. (row 2038)

Eurodollar University adds a second measure. It says PIMCO calculates a "shadow default rate" of 19% on about $500 billion held in retail-oriented BDCs. (row 2544)

One counter-example exists in the cards. Ares Capital reported non-accruals of $708 million in Q2, still below its 3% historical average. (row 2071) The Blue Owl loan to Loparex fell from par to near zero within months. (row 2044) That claim is Partly supported. OBDC's non-accruals were only about 0.8% of portfolio fair value, so one loan says little about the wider book. (row 2044)

Redemption gates and funding

Redemption limits are the clearest change in the argument. In March 2026 Blackstone's BCRED met 7% of 8% requested withdrawals. (row 2311) By June 2026 it capped payouts at 5% against 10% requested. (row 1337) In September 2026 Eurodollar University said the cap held for a second quarter. (row 2048) Apollo Debt Solutions faced requests for 14.7% of shares in its third gated quarter. (row 2544) Blue Owl Technology Income Corp. saw requests for 39% in Q3. (rows 2984, 3221)

Eurodollar University argues the warning starts with funding, not defaults. In July 2026 it said HSBC would not renew some credit lines to private credit funds. (row 2088) The Financial Stability Board counts about $220 billion of bank credit lines to these funds. Commercial estimates run to more than twice that. (row 2071)

Submitted interviews with Edward Dowd say bank lending to non-banks became the marginal credit engine, and that engine is now frozen. (rows 1371, 2836) Boyle noted in October 2025 that lending to non-bank financial firms made up all of that year's bank loan growth. (row 1851)

Insurers form a related channel. Delaware Life and Clear Spring disclosed more than $20 billion of loans that should have been classed as affiliated. (rows 2038, 2054) Federal grand jury subpoenas followed. (row 2079)

AI debt as the next credit risk

From May 2026 the channels linked bank stress to AI financing. Tom Bilyeu's channel cited the Financial Times: banks were offloading AI data-center debt to pension funds, insurers and private credit. (row 2218) Felix & Friends said one in five lending dollars now goes to AI. That figure has no outside source in the card. (row 2254)

Market prices gave support in late 2026. Oracle's credit default swap reached about 215 basis points in July, from about 145 at the end of 2025. (row 2072) By October Felix & Friends put it at 244 basis points. (row 3146) A guest on Bilyeu's channel disagreed in August. Hyperscalers carry debt equal to only 4% of market cap, and their cash flow covers interest. (row 2188)

Consumers and mortgages

Boyle's October 2025 post set the tone. Fitch showed 6.6% of subprime auto loans in securitised pools 60 or more days past due, the highest on record. (row 1851) That is Supported. The index covers only securitised subprime pools, and prime auto delinquency stayed near 0.37%.

The G.19 data drew opposing readings. Eurodollar University said households hit their borrowing limit. Revolving credit fell by more than $5 billion in May 2026, and rose only $2.8 billion in July. (rows 2043, 2087) The claim is Partly supported. Revolving balances reached a record of about $1.357 trillion in July, which sits awkwardly with a borrowing limit. Revolving credit fell $4.8 billion again in August. (row 3142)

The delinquency figures differ by speaker. RE-V cited the New York Fed for 13% of card balances over 90 days past due. (row 1321) A guest on ITM Trading said 18% of the population is 90 days late. (row 3272) ITM Trading sells the precious metals it discusses.

RE-V reported mortgage delinquency of 4.4% in Q1 2026 and FHA delinquency of 11.88%. (rows 1322, 1319) RE-V also noted serious delinquency of 1%, far below the 5% of 2009-2010. (row 1382) Florida's delinquencies had returned only to 2017-2019 levels. (row 1353)

Commercial property and lending standards

The Timeless Investor focused on commercial real estate in January 2026. It cited $957 billion of loans maturing that year, with 14% estimated underwater. (row 2703) It cited office CMBS delinquency of 11.76%. (row 2714) It says regulators endorsed "extend and pretend". (row 2714) A submitted video in July 2026 described buildings trading at 80 cents on the dollar. (row 1372)

On standards, the picture is mixed. The administration loosened capital rules in 2026, and the March re-proposal was lighter. (rows 2207, 2678) Eurodollar University argues that banks in Europe and China tightened and bought government bonds instead of lending. (rows 2078, 2051) It also argues that the US shows the same pattern. (row 2066)

How the argument changed

In October 2025 the focus was single frauds, Tricolor and First Brands. (row 1851) In early 2026 it moved to commercial property maturities. (row 2709) From March 2026 it became private-credit gates. By September and October 2026 the channels said stress had reached public credit. Eurodollar University put triple-C spreads near 1,300 basis points in October. (rows 3221, 3303)

Tom Bilyeu's channel and a submitted 2024 video argue that banks create money when they lend. (rows 2198, 1458) This view treats credit contraction as a loss of money itself. (row 2189)

What to watch

  • Fitch's private-credit default rate and the share of extensions. (rows 2038, 2071)
  • Redemption requests against the 5% caps at BCRED, Apollo and Blue Owl. (rows 2048, 2544)
  • Triple-C spreads: 1,300 basis points, then 1,500. (row 2969)
  • Bank credit lines to private credit funds. (rows 2071, 2088)
  • Oracle and CoreWeave default-swap prices. (rows 3146, 3394)
  • Monthly G.19 revolving credit. (rows 2043, 3142)

Jobs and growth

Labor market: fragile, resilient or distorted?

The channels agree that hiring is weak. They disagree on what the weakness means. RE-V said in February 2026 that hiring was at its worst level since 2008 (row 1368). In March 2026 it cited a loss of 92,000 jobs in February 2026 (row 1361). Bilyeu's channel said in July 2026 that the annual benchmark revision cut 2025 job growth from 584,000 to 181,000 (row 2200).

Eurodollar University argues the labor market is fragile, not resilient. It cited a payroll fall of 23,000 in July 2026 (rows 2067, 2065). It said revisions removed 103,000 jobs from May and June (row 2055). It said participation fell to 61.4% and that effective unemployment is near 6.2%, against the official 4.1% (row 2055). In October 2026 it said the US was 9.7 million jobs short of the 2010s trend (row 2985). Bilyeu's channel repeated that figure and cited 29,000 September jobs against 84,000 expected (row 3082). Upside Invest noted that August 2026 added 162,000 jobs, above expectations (row 2592).

Other channels point the other way. Warsh called unemployment of 4.1-4.2% very low, as ITM Trading, a precious-metals dealer, reported in August 2026 (row 3276). Patrick Boyle said in May 2026 that Federal Reserve banks estimate break-even payroll growth has roughly halved since early 2024 (row 1821). The fact-check rates this Partly supported. Estimates vary with immigration assumptions. The St. Louis Fed's 2026 range spans 15,000 to 87,000. A low break-even may therefore show weak labor supply, not a tight market (row 1821).

Households appear worried. Eurodollar University cited the New York Fed survey for August 2026. It showed a 44.4% chance of higher unemployment a year ahead, the highest since April 2020 (rows 2041, 2042, 2043). The fact-check rates this Partly supported. The same release showed job-loss expectations falling to 13.8%, the lowest since February 2026 (rows 2041, 2042, 2043). One video said 40% of Americans cannot raise $400 in an emergency (row 2864). The fact-check rates this Contradicted. The Fed survey share was 37% in 2025 (row 2864).

AI is a second labor argument. RE-V said in April 2026 that Block cut 40% of staff and blamed AI (rows 1356, 1357). Upside Invest reported in September 2026 that Uber cut 3,300 jobs (row 2604). Bilyeu's channel cited Robert Half in August 2026: 29% to 32% of firms that cut jobs for AI have begun to restaff (row 2190).

GDP and AI investment

Most channels say AI spending now carries US growth. Harvard's Jason Furman calculated that AI investment made up about 90% of US growth in the first half of 2025 (rows 1805, 2185). The fact-check rates this Supported. Furman said it is not a counterfactual. Lower rates and power prices could have offset about half of it (rows 1805, 2185). Peak Prosperity said in August 2026 that about 50% of first-quarter 2026 growth came from AI capex (row 3345). RE-V gave a similar share (row 1320). Timeless Investor noted in December 2025 that 2025 growth was tracking 2.5% (row 2715). The Fed projects 2.3% real growth for 2026 (row 2177).

The argument moved from valuation to financing. In October 2025, Boyle worried about circular deals. He also noted that big tech would generate over $200 billion of free cash flow after capex (row 1848). By mid-2026 the focus was debt. Eurodollar University said AI-related debt issuance reached about $270 billion by July 2026 (row 2079). It said Google's free cash flow turned negative, at $5.9 billion, in the second quarter (row 2077). Bilyeu's channel said hyperscaler free cash flow fell below zero in 2026 (row 2190).

Several figures come from named institutions. The Wall Street Journal found about $3 trillion of AI commitments in footnotes, five times reported capex of about $600 billion (rows 1805, 2185). The fact-check rates this Supported. Much of it sits in normal contracts already disclosed, and Morgan Stanley's accountants called it hard to gauge, not hidden (rows 1805, 2185). Morgan Stanley estimates $1.5 trillion of outside financing by 2028 (rows 1371, 2215, 3112). This is Partly supported. Morgan Stanley itself expects no financing bottleneck (rows 1371, 2215, 3112). Reuters reported that Anthropic's S-1 showed 2025 revenue of $4.6 billion and an $8 billion operating loss (rows 2886, 2986). This is Partly supported. The $42 billion total loss includes about $34 billion of accounting charges, and $518 billion of obligations are real (rows 2886, 2986, 3006). OpenAI told investors in September 2026 that annualized revenue neared $50 billion, against about $70 billion reported days earlier (rows 3145, 3171). The fact-check rates this Supported. The gap may reflect differing definitions (rows 3145, 3171).

Boyle, Bilyeu and Peak Prosperity call the build-out a bubble. Boyle also cited estimates that an AI correction would erase tens of trillions of dollars (row 1805). This is Supported and conditional. Upside Invest points to strong demand, such as Samsung's $80 billion third-quarter profit (row 3141). The Fed's September 2026 minutes named the data-center boom as a force keeping prices high (row 3113). This is Supported, though tariffs and energy costs appear first in the minutes (row 3113).

Recession risk

Eurodollar University argues that an energy shock is destroying demand (rows 2049, 2384). It says retail sales fell in July 2026 after temporary highs (row 2061). Reuters, cited by RE-V, put the July fall at 0.6% (row 1621). The Conference Board's index fell to 89.4 in August 2026, with expectations at 68.2 (row 2055). In September it reached its lowest level since 2014, with expectations at 63.6 (row 2912). The fact-check rates this Supported. The sub-80 reading has persisted since February 2025 without a recession, so the threshold has given false signals (rows 2041, 2055, 2912, 3142).

Some data cut the other way. Real per-capita consumer spending rose 2% in the second quarter of 2026 (row 1955). Manufacturing output fell 0.3% in August 2026 (row 2384). This is Partly supported. The core figure matches the Fed's first estimate. The automaker remark is unverified (row 2384). RE-V argued in September 2026 that AI capex keeps unemployment capped (row 1774). Warsh said inflation has run above 2% for 65 months, with PCE at 3.7% (row 1804). This is Supported.

Trade and tariffs

In July 2025, a submitted video noted 15% US tariffs on EU goods and a 2024 trade deficit of $915 billion (row 53). In February 2026, Boyle reported that the Supreme Court struck down about two-thirds of the tariffs. He gave the 2025 goods deficit as a record $1.2 trillion (row 1830). He cited New York Fed research that Americans bore 94% of the tariff cost from January to August 2025, and 86% by November (row 1830). This is Supported. The administration disputed the study, and the method cannot split the share between consumers and firms (row 1830).

Boyle cited the IMF: internal EU barriers equal a 44% tariff on goods and 110% on services (row 1819). This is Partly supported. Critics say language, distance and preferences explain most of the gap (row 1819). Boyle cited Bloomberg that energy and lost exports each explain 40% of Germany's GDP shortfall (rows 1812, 2281). This is Supported. Eurodollar University and Boyle both put Europe's deficit with China near €1 billion a day (rows 1812, 2074). Upside Invest cited industry estimates that chip tariffs would cost about $90 billion a year in GDP (row 2951).

  • Labor force participation, at 61.4% in July 2026 (row 2055).

Inflation

The energy shock drives the headline

Most channels say the Iran war caused the 2026 price surge. Patrick Boyle said in May 2026 that the assault shut about 20 million barrels a day and pushed Brent above $125 a barrel (row 1821). Felix & Friends said in April 2026 that US gasoline was up 38% since the war began (row 2304). Upside Invest said in September 2026 that gasoline averaged $4.27 a gallon, up 44% (row 2592).

Channels also cite tanker attacks and oil forecasts. Peak Prosperity said at least 12 tankers were hit near Hormuz in the week to 5 October 2026. It said this was the most since the war began (row 3316). Felix & Friends said Goldman Sachs models oil at $150 a barrel (rows 2267, 2271). Fact-check: Partly supported. Goldman did publish a $160 peak scenario in March 2026. Brent's October high of about $136 is closer to that scenario than to Goldman's base case (rows 2267, 2271, 3316).

The consumer price path

The 2026 path rose, fell, then rose again. November 2025 CPI was 2.7% (row 2715). In March 2026, Felix & Friends put inflation at 2.4%. It said economists saw 3.5% or more (row 2314). Tom Bilyeu cited the Bureau of Labor Statistics: April CPI was 3.8%, and producer prices rose 6% (row 2222). Patrick Boyle gave the same figures (row 1817). A directly submitted video said May CPI was 4.2% (row 1140).

June CPI fell. Eurodollar University said prices dropped nearly half a percent in the month. It said the annual rate fell to about 3.5% (row 2084). Peak Prosperity said PPI eased to 5.5% in July (row 3359). Then August CPI was 3.4% (rows 2592, 2647). September CPI was 3.7% (rows 3243, 3361).

Channels give different core figures. Peak Prosperity put core CPI at 2.6% in July (row 3359). Eurodollar University put it at 2.4% for August (row 2042). Upside Invest gave 3.3% core in late August (row 2955). The cards do not say if the measures differ.

Fact-check on the official record. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at Jackson Hole that inflation had run above 2% for 65 months. He put the Fed's preferred PCE measure at 3.7%. Verdict: Supported (rows 1804, 2050). Patrick Boyle also cited New York Fed research that Americans bore 94% of the 2025 tariff cost from January to August. The share fell to 86% by November. Verdict: Supported. The administration disputed the study. The import-price method cannot split the share between consumers and importers (row 1830).

Demand destruction or lasting inflation?

Eurodollar University argues the shock destroys demand. It says core CPI turned fractionally negative in June 2026 (row 2084). It says TIPS break-evens fell to their lowest since October 2024 in July (row 2073). It says August gasoline demand was 8.9 million barrels a day, below 9.05 million a year earlier (row 2049). It says energy shocks differ from persistent monetary inflation (row 2053).

Peak Prosperity disagrees. It argues official CPI understates costs. It says the BLS showed fuel oil up 39.1% year on year in July. It puts the real rise near 100% (row 3342). It cites Charlie Bilello: coffee was up 127% over seven years (row 3359). In August it expected a 6% CPI print around September to October (row 3345). ITM Trading argued in October that a second inflation wave echoes 1966–1982 (row 3245). ITM Trading sells the precious metals it discusses.

Crude versus products, and manipulation claims

Channels agree that diesel is the tightest market. Eurodollar University said the diesel crack spread passed $100 a barrel in September 2026, a record (row 2049). Upside Invest said diesel reached $6.50 a gallon (row 2945). Eurodollar University reads this as a refining bottleneck, not a crude shortage (row 2082). Doomberg blames Russian refinery damage (row 2539).

They disagree on what futures show. Peak Prosperity argues futures are manipulated. In October it cited dated Brent at $126.89 against futures at $101.65 (row 3319). It cited Chris Martenson, who put the real oil price at $130–$150 (row 3258). Eurodollar University reads the flat back end of the curve as weak long-term demand (row 2075).

Food costs

Food claims focus on fertiliser and diesel. Patrick Boyle said in April 2026 that anhydrous ammonia rose from $800 to $1,050 a ton. He cited a Farm Bureau survey: about 70% of farmers could not afford all their fertiliser (row 1822). Peak Prosperity said food at home rose 33% from 2019 to June 2026 (row 3348). It also warned of a food crunch in August (row 3341). Other cards show retail price cuts. Walmart cut prices on more than 11,000 items (row 2049). Pepsi cut prices by up to 15% (row 2855).

Expectations

Survey and market measures point different ways. The New York Fed survey put one-year expectations at 3.58% and five-year expectations at 3% (row 2043). Fact-check: Partly supported. The August survey showed the mean chance of higher unemployment at 44.4%, a high since April 2020. Job-loss expectations fell to 13.8% in the same release (rows 2041, 2042, 2043). The University of Michigan one-year figure rose from 4% to 4.6% in September (row 2734). Tom Bilyeu said bonds priced 2.3% inflation over ten years (row 2647). Eurodollar University said TIPS price near-zero risk in October (row 2985).

Policy views shifted. In July 2026, Bessent called inflation a supply shock (row 2050). The Fed's own view hardened. Fact-check: Supported. The Fed expects inflation above 2% until 2029 and names AI investment. Only the minutes link AI to prices; tariffs and energy are cited first (row 3113). Upside Invest said the Fed hiked once in September (row 2563).

Channels disagree on cause. Tom Bilyeu said in July that 2021–2022 was mainly a supply shock (row 2202). Peak Prosperity said money creation caused it (row 3324). Felix & Friends cited M2 near $23 trillion (row 2893). Fact-check: Supported. M2 grew $868 billion in calendar 2025, above the $600 billion the video gave for last year (row 2893).

  • PPI, with its four-to-six month lag to CPI (rows 3345, 2222).
  • New York Fed and Michigan expectations surveys (rows 2043, 2734).
