Markets and the dollar

Concentration and valuation

Most channels argue that US stocks now depend on a few AI companies. Felix & Friends says the top 10 stocks make up about 40% of the S&P 500 and drove 72% of 2026 gains (rows 2232, 2269). It cites JPMorgan for AI stocks at 49% of the index in October 2026, up from 26% in early 2023 (row 3146). Tom Bilyeu says the Shiller CAPE crossed 40 in May 2026, against a long-run average near 17 (row 2222). Edward Dowd, in videos submitted directly, puts AI and AI-adjacent names at 45% of the S&P 500 (rows 1596, 2836).

Morgan Stanley found that about 89% of Russell 3000 stocks were down more than 10% from their June 2026 peaks. Fact-check: Supported. Morgan Stanley's note is not public, so the full breakdown rests on one press report (rows 3146, 3361). Peak Prosperity separately says 59% of S&P 500 members were at least 20% below their highs in October 2026 (rows 3320, 3316).

Jeremy Grantham, quoted by Bilyeu in July 2026, argues AI stocks could fall 70% (row 2206). Other voices are less severe. Patrick Boyle noted in October 2025 that AI leaders traded near 35 times forward earnings, against 60 times for late-1990s internet stocks (row 1848). Boyle cited Bloomberg in September 2026 for Nvidia at under 17 times expected profit (row 2732). Felix & Friends put the Nasdaq 100 at 21 times forward profit in October 2026, against about 200 times for Cisco in 2000 (row 3394). Upside Invest reports that about one in three of its tracked investors owns Nvidia, with mostly buys (rows 2603, 2940). Goldman Sachs upgraded stocks to overweight in October 2026 (row 3202).

Who pays for the AI build-out

Debt is the central bubble argument. Eurodollar University argues the boom finances physical assets with debt, private credit and leases (row 2065). Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in Q2 2026, its first since 2004 (rows 2077, 2072). Bilyeu says hyperscaler bond issuance rose from $20 billion in 2024 to $110 billion in 2025 and $150 billion in 2026 (row 2190). He also says hyperscaler debt-to-value was 4%, against 30% at the dot-com peak (row 2190).

Morgan Stanley estimates AI needs about $1.5 trillion of outside financing by 2028. Fact-check: Partly supported. Morgan Stanley itself said it does not expect a financing bottleneck, because credit markets can absorb the issuance (rows 1371, 2215, 3112).

A Wall Street Journal analysis found about $3 trillion of AI commitments in filing footnotes, roughly five times reported capex of about $600 billion. Fact-check: Supported. Much of it sits in normal contracts that are already disclosed, and Morgan Stanley accountants called it hard to gauge, not hidden (rows 1805, 2185). Michael Burry, in September 2026, gave the same $3 trillion split into $1.2 trillion of leases and $1.5 trillion of purchase commitments (row 2568). Burry also argues chip lives of two to three years, not five to six, hide losses (rows 2211, 2973).

Anthropic's S-1, as reported by Reuters, showed 2025 revenue of $4.6 billion, an $8 billion operating loss and a $42 billion total loss. Fact-check: Partly supported. The filing lists $518 billion of mostly non-cancellable compute obligations, so the losses are real even without the paper charge (rows 2886, 2986). Upside Invest says about $34 billion of the loss is an accounting charge on convertible financing (row 3006).

In October 2026 OpenAI told investors its annualised revenue was near $50 billion, about $20 billion below the figure reported days earlier. Fact-check: Supported. The gap may reflect different revenue definitions (rows 3145, 3171). Bilyeu says $370 billion of market value fell in one session (row 3145).

The credit channel also draws attention. Fitch data show US private-credit default rates at records in mid-2026. Fact-check: Partly supported. Most "defaults" are negotiated amendments, and the index began only in August 2024 (rows 2038, 2071). Blue Owl marked a Loparex loan to near zero. Fact-check: Partly supported. Blue Owl's non-accruals were only about 0.8% of its portfolio (row 2044).

How the argument changed

In late 2025 the debate was about circular financing (rows 1848, 1844, 2973). In February and March 2026 the Iran war dominated. Felix & Friends said on 28 February that the S&P typically falls 5–7% in ten days, then recovers (row 2321). On 30 March it said every major oil spike in 50 years preceded a crash (row 2306). Boyle noted in April 2026 that the S&P had hit a record despite the war (row 1822).

From May 2026 the focus moved to froth. Bank of America, via Felix & Friends, said semiconductors traded 60% above their 200-day average (row 2279). The SpaceX IPO then raised $75 billion in June (row 1815). By July the mood turned. South Korea's KOSPI fell about 27% from its June peak (row 1810). The MSCI World Semiconductor Index fell 16% in July (row 2072). By October the worry was a Fed rate rise and OpenAI's revenue miss (rows 2563, 3145).

The dollar: erosion or strength

Felix & Friends, The Timeless Investor and ITM Trading argue that the dollar is losing its reserve role. They put its reserve share at about 57–58%, down from 71% (rows 2710, 2299). The channels do not agree on the level. Felix & Friends cites a central-bank survey at 42% (row 2263). ITM Trading, a precious-metals dealer that sells the metals it discusses, says 54% (row 3286). On purchasing power since 1971, the channels cite losses of 85% (row 3285), 88% (row 2234), 93% (row 2726) and 99% (row 2236).

Eurodollar University disagrees. It cites BIS data that the dollar's share of FX contracts was unchanged or higher through 2025 (row 2052). It argues private dollar conditions in Asia stay tight even when the Dollar Index slips below 100 (rows 2052, 2076).

Foreign official institutions cut New York Fed custody holdings by $346.2 billion. Fact-check: Partly supported. Custody holdings are only part of foreign holdings, and central banks can move Treasuries to private custodians (rows 2083, 2276).

Boyle said in February 2026 that the dollar had weakened about 10% in a year (row 1830). Felix & Friends said the DXY gained about 6% when the war began (row 2303). Felix & Friends cites Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan for a further 10% fall (row 2276).

Yen and Asian currencies

Yen intervention drew the most attention in July and August 2026. Japan spent $73 billion in April and May (rows 2248, 2196). The Ministry of Finance used 15.4 trillion yen ($96.4 billion) between 30 July and 26 August (row 2052). The US intervened on 31 July for the first time since 1998 (rows 1806, 2052). Eurodollar University argues each rally fades because outflows from Japanese institutions drive the carry trade (rows 2086, 2070). Felix & Friends sizes the carry trade at $1–20 trillion (row 2248).

Gold and money supply

Goldman Sachs forecast gold at $4,900 an ounce by end-2026. Fact-check: Supported. Goldman cut the forecast to $4,650 on 23 September 2026 as Fed hikes weighed (rows 2229, 2236, 2248). Several channels say central banks buy gold at a record pace above 1,000 tonnes a year. Fact-check: Partly supported. Q2 2026 buying set a second-quarter record, but 2022–2024 buying was the strongest on records back to 1950 (rows 2679, 2227, 2228, 2230).

US M2 reached about $23 trillion and is growing at its fastest pace since 2022. Fact-check: Supported. Full-year 2025 growth was $868 billion, above the video's $600 billion (row 2893). The Fed expects inflation above 2% until 2029. Fact-check: Supported. The projections do not mention AI. Only the minutes link AI to prices (row 3113).

What to watch

  • Shiller CAPE near or above 40, and the share of stocks 20% below their highs (rows 2222, 3320).
  • Hyperscaler free cash flow and bond issuance (rows 2190, 2072).
  • Credit default swap spreads at Oracle and CoreWeave (rows 2071, 3361).
  • Private-credit default rates and Blue Owl marks (rows 2038, 2044).
  • Nvidia earnings on 18 November 2026 (row 3545).
  • OpenAI and Anthropic revenue and IPO timing (rows 3145, 2886).
  • SpaceX lock-up expiries from 11 August 2026 (row 2264).
  • The yen near 160 per dollar and further intervention (rows 2052, 2196).
  • Dollar reserve share and New York Fed custody holdings (rows 2299, 2276).
  • Central-bank gold buying (row 2679).

Commodities and metals

Gold: a war trade that crashed, then a central-bank bid

Felix & Friends argued in February and March 2026 that gold gains after oil shocks. It cited Bank of America: gold beats most assets by 19% six months after a shock (row 2321). It also cited 1979, when gold rose 276% in one year (row 2319).

Gold then fell. It peaked above $5,500 an ounce on 29 January 2026 and dropped to about $4,000, down 28% (row 2204). Felix & Friends blamed forced selling, not weak demand. It named CME margin changes and sales by Turkey and Gulf states (rows 2303, 2307). Turkey sold about 60 tons in two weeks (row 2307). Axel Merk, a guest on ITM Trading in October 2026, argued that an oil shock hurts gold unless policymakers respond with inflation (row 3250). ITM Trading said Treasury yields reached 5.44%, the highest in over 20 years (row 3253). Verdict: Partly supported. If the speaker meant the 10-year note, the figure is wrong. It closed at 5.26% on the upload date and never exceeded 5.31% (row 3253).

By September 2026 gold traded between $4,300 and $4,700 (rows 3260, 2281).

Central-bank buying: agreed in direction, not in size

Most gold-focused channels say central banks buy about 1,000 tons a year, roughly double the pre-2022 rate (rows 2230, 2263). Verdict: Partly supported. Buying of 289 tonnes in Q2 2026 set a second-quarter record, so the pace may be rising again. The 2022–2024 buying was the strongest in World Gold Council records back to 1950 (rows 2204, 2227, 2228, 2230).

The channels disagree on the total. Felix & Friends gave 900 tons, "almost 1,000" and 1,050 tons for last year in different videos (rows 2323, 2297, 2303). Peak Prosperity gave 20–30 tons a month since 2024, which is far lower (row 3349). Tom Bilyeu cited 244 tons in the first quarter of 2026, the strongest first quarter on record (row 2204).

China is the focus. ITM Trading guests said China imported over 1,100 tons by August 2026 (row 3256). Goldman Sachs speculates that China's holdings are nearly double the reported figure (row 3249). Several channels say gold now exceeds Treasuries in official reserves (rows 3349, 3244).

Price targets

Goldman Sachs forecast gold at $4,900 by end-2026, about 20% above prevailing prices (rows 2229, 2236, 2248). Verdict: Supported. Goldman said the target needs easier rates, a weaker dollar and investor inflows, not only central-bank demand. It cut the forecast to $4,650 on 23 September 2026 as Fed hikes weighed (rows 2229, 2236, 2248).

Felix & Friends gave a JP Morgan target of $4,500 in July 2026 and $6,000 in September 2026 (rows 2248, 2229). ITM Trading is a precious-metals dealer and sells the metals it discusses. Its guests forecast $10,000 (Jim Rickards) and $13,000 by 2030 (Gareth Soloway) (rows 3276, 3269). Soloway also expected sideways trading to year-end (row 3269).

Silver: deficit story, then a challenge to the squeeze story

Felix & Friends said in February 2026 that Comex registered silver fell from 120 million ounces to 88 million. It said paper claims outnumber metal 365 to 1 (row 2323). It reported silver above $100 in March (row 2314). A January record near $125 was reported later (row 2258).

The same channel changed course in March 2026. It said real leverage is about 7 times, not 350 times (row 2309). It put the chance of a managed squeeze at 30–50% (row 2309). Peak Prosperity said a 12% Chinese import tax explains the Shanghai price gap (row 3315). The March video had called the gap a 19% premium from capital controls (row 2309). All sources agree on a multi-year deficit, which Goldman Sachs also noted (row 3315).

By August and September 2026, silver traded near $54–$55. Soloway said it could fall to $50 if the economy weakens (rows 3291, 3269).

Copper and other metals

Felix & Friends cited J.P. Morgan: copper at $12,500 by Q2 2026, and 500,000 tons of data-centre demand this year (rows 2317, 2289). Verdict: Partly supported. The $12,500 target was J.P. Morgan's published view when stated in March 2026 (row 2317).

The International Copper Study Group sees a deficit of 150,000 tons (row 2317). In September 2026 Felix & Friends cited Bloomberg for a deficit of about one million tonnes after a roughly 40% one-year price rise (row 2281). Verdict: Supported. Goldman Sachs forecast a 300,000-tonne surplus for 2026, so one million tonnes is the top of the range (row 2281).

China's grip on supply is a second theme. Patrick Boyle said in November 2025 that China supplies about 80% of rare earths and refines over 90% (row 1847). Tom Bilyeu said in August 2026 that China refines about 98% of gallium and germanium (row 2187). Eurodollar University said iron ore fell to about $91 a ton in October 2026, a four-year low (row 3161). Only one guest discussed platinum. Dave Collum, on ITM Trading, argued that above-ground platinum could run out in two or three years (row 3556).

Oil: physical shortage or demand destruction

All channels agree that Hormuz carries about a fifth of seaborne oil (rows 2304, 3258). Brent rose from about $60 early in 2026 to over $120, then settled near $86–$87 in August 2026 (row 3285). Oil topped $100 again in September (row 2592).

Peak Prosperity argues that futures are managed down. In October 2026 it cited dated Brent at $126.89 against futures at $101.65 (row 3319). It said the world is missing about 12 million barrels a day (row 3356). It predicted in July 2026 that prices would soon explode (row 3355).

Eurodollar University reads the same data as weak demand. It said China's June imports fell about 41% (row 2082). It cited an IEA forecast of a 2.5 million barrel-a-day fall in 2026 demand (row 2042). Doomberg, in submitted videos, said refinery damage explains why crude lags products (row 2539).

Boyle cited Trafigura: a loss of 1.5 billion barrels of Gulf crude is almost unavoidable (row 1822). Peak Prosperity said at least 12 tankers were hit around Hormuz in the week to 5 October 2026 (row 3316). Felix & Friends said Goldman Sachs modeled oil at $150 a barrel or more (rows 2267, 2271). Verdict: Partly supported. Goldman published a $160 peak scenario in March 2026. Brent's October high near $136 is closer to it than to Goldman's base case (rows 2267, 2271, 3316).

Gas and refined fuels

Boyle said in March 2026 that Qatar supplies a fifth of world LNG (row 1826). The Qatari energy minister said 17% of capacity will be out for three to five years (row 1826). Diesel is now the main stress point. Diesel crack spreads passed $100 a barrel in early September 2026 (row 2049). US distillate stocks were 103 million barrels, the lowest for the season in EIA records (row 2049). US diesel hit a record $6.50 a gallon in late September (row 2945).

Food and farm goods

Peak Prosperity links energy to food. It said sulfur exports fell 80% (row 3338). Boyle said a third of seaborne fertilizer passes Hormuz (row 1826). The USDA put the US cattle herd at 86.2 million head, the lowest since the 1950s (row 3341). Eurodollar University said Australian farm diesel cost over 50% more year on year (row 3117). Felix & Friends argued in October 2026 that an oil price collapse would cut costs across the economy (row 2915).

What to watch

  • Hormuz tanker traffic and attacks (rows 3316, 3343).
  • Dated Brent against futures (rows 3319, 3320).
  • Diesel crack spreads and US distillate stocks (rows 2049, 3338).
  • US Strategic Petroleum Reserve and Cushing stocks (rows 2535, 3347).
  • Central-bank gold purchases, especially China's (rows 3249, 3256).
  • Comex registered silver and gold inventories (rows 2323, 2320).
  • Treasury yields and the dollar (rows 3253, 2310).
  • Copper balance forecasts (row 2281).
  • Fertilizer and sulfur flows (rows 3338, 2228).

Regional differences

RE-V supplies almost all the US state and metro figures in these cards. (rows 1360, 1349) The other channels mostly discuss other countries. (rows 2078, 2194) RE-V also cites its own ReVenture app for several local figures. (rows 1360, 2419)

A market split in two

RE-V argues that the US housing market has split in two. (row 1355) In February 2026, RE-V cited National Association of Realtors (NAR) data. West Coast prices were down 1.4% year over year. (row 1367) Northeast prices were up 5.8%, Midwest prices up 2.3%, and South prices flat. (row 1367)

In March 2026, RE-V gave year-over-year declines of 2% in Georgia, 5% in Florida, 3% in Texas and 2% in Arizona. (row 1360) In April 2026, it named Wisconsin and North Dakota (both up 5.1%) and Illinois (up 4.5%) as growth leaders. (row 1355) In August 2026, it gave North Dakota 5.3% and New York 5.2%. (row 1406)

At metro level, RE-V says Austin fell 24.6% from mid-2022 to April 2026. (row 1351) Over the same period, it says Rockford, Illinois rose 32% and Syracuse, New York rose 31%. (row 1351) RE-V reported a Chicago price forecast of +6.2% and a Denver forecast of −8.8% in July 2026. (row 1327)

The channel also finds splits inside single metros. It says north Dallas pockets gain 5–7% a year, while pockets 2–3 miles south lose 9% a year. (row 1325) It cites J.P. Morgan for the claim that about half of US states had falling values in July 2026. (row 1325)

Affordability and supply explain the split

RE-V links the split to cost. In May 2026 it said buying in California takes 62% of median household income. (row 1349) Florida needs 48%. (row 1349) Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky, Indiana and Iowa stay below 30%. (row 1349)

West Coast price-to-rent ratios run at 19X to 20X, against 10X to 12X in the Midwest and South (May 2026). (row 1340) RE-V says Idaho's price-to-income ratio passed 5 in June 2026, a record. (row 1339)

Supply matters too. RE-V says Chicago has 14,000 homes for sale, down from 40,000 before the pandemic. (row 1406) It says Seattle has more than 12,000 listings, 65% above the July long-term average. (row 1406)

How the argument changed

Early in 2026, RE-V framed the weakness as a Texas and Florida problem. In May 2026, it said the largest inventory surpluses had moved to Tennessee, Colorado, Washington, Arizona, Nevada, the Carolinas and Georgia. (row 1348) By July 2026, it added Utah, Oregon and Washington, D.C. (row 1329)

The Zillow forecast list also grew. In March 2026, it named Dallas, Houston, Washington D.C., San Francisco, Seattle, Denver and San Antonio. (row 1358) In May 2026, RE-V added Los Angeles, Atlanta, Phoenix and Minneapolis, with declines expected by March 2027. (row 1349)

From late August 2026, RE-V turned to tech hubs and the Northeast. It said Boston would be the first Northeast market to crack, in the second half of 2026. (row 1607) In September 2026 it reported Raleigh led the US for sales declines, and San Diego sales fell 43% from the pandemic peak. (rows 2327, 2009)

Where the claims conflict

San Francisco is the clearest conflict. In April 2026, RE-V said Oakland values fell 25% in 3.5 years. (row 1350) In May 2026, it cited Redfin: San Francisco pending sales rose over 15% year over year. (row 1346) Zillow data for May 2026 showed San Francisco County up 1.2% month over month while Seattle and Austin fell. (row 1330)

In August 2026, RE-V reported the highest San Francisco median rent in nearly a decade, $3,700 a month. (row 1572) A video submitted directly in July 2026 instead said urban cores such as San Francisco, Seattle and Portland face headwinds. (row 1372) That video noted rent growth in some New York pockets. (row 1372)

Cape Coral shows a second conflict. The Wall Street Journal called it the worst US market. (row 1616) RE-V called it undervalued in August 2026, and said sales passed 2,000 in June. (row 1616) In September 2026, RE-V still reported losses of 30–40% for some sellers. (row 1956)

Florida as the stress centre

From June 2026, RE-V focused on Florida. It cites Adam Data for one foreclosure per 2,100 housing units, the highest rate of any state. (row 1332) Arizona's foreclosures rose 76% in the year, at one per 2,600 units. (row 1332)

Redfin data, cited in June 2026, put investor purchases down 77% in Jacksonville and 73% in Atlanta. (row 1336) Punta Gorda values are down 27% from peak. (row 1800) Yet Miami-Dade values are up 12.6% since mid-2022. (row 1600) RE-V says Miami rents stay high while central and western Florida rents fall. (row 2418)

RE-V also names places that resisted. It says Oklahoma City avoided the 2008 downturn. (row 1645) It credits oil prices for Alaska's price strength in September 2026. (row 1914) ReVenture calls New Orleans the most undervalued US market. (row 2032)

Other countries

RE-V presents the US correction as international. In May 2026, it cited the Royal Bank of Canada: Canadian prices were down nearly 20% from the 2022 peak. (row 1344) In June 2026, it put New Zealand down 16%. (row 1339) It gave England a price-to-income ratio of 7.7. (row 1339) It gave Catania, Sicily a ratio of 4.1. (row 1341)

Patrick Boyle cites the Financial Times: about 66,000 New Zealanders left for Australia in the year to June 2026. (row 1816) He also cites it for a 14% hit to British living standards if London were removed. (row 1813)

Eurodollar University argues in July 2026 that Europe has fallen behind the US over nearly 20 years. (row 2078) It cites a German Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey: almost one-fifth of 3,000+ firms weighed cutting German capacity or moving abroad. (row 2074) Peak Prosperity says German energy-intensive industry is 28% below its peak. (row 3337) A submitted Doomberg interview in September 2026 says Europe uses 11 million barrels of oil but produces 300,000. (row 2539)

On China, the channels disagree. Tom Bilyeu's guest Steve Keen argued in August 2026 that China grew income about 8% a year since 1980, against 2% for America. (row 2194) A submitted Edward Dowd interview in September 2026 says China's GDP in dollars fell from 80% to 60% of US GDP. (row 2836) Dowd also says its real estate starts are down 70% since 2021. (row 2836)

Eurodollar University reported falls in international air traffic of 6% in Cancun, 8% in Los Cabos and 20% in Puerto Vallarta (September 2026). (row 2384) Tom Bilyeu and ITM Trading, a precious-metals dealer, discuss immigration in Sweden and Spain, not housing. (rows 2224, 3287)

What to watch

  • Foreclosures per housing unit by state, especially Florida and Arizona. (row 1332)
  • Investor purchases by metro, which Redfin data shows down about 70% in several Sunbelt cities. (row 1518)
  • Inventory surplus by state, and listings against pre-pandemic levels. (rows 1348, 1406)
  • Zillow metro forecasts through 2027. (row 1349)
  • Price-to-income and price-to-rent ratios by region. (rows 1339, 1340)
  • Rent changes by metro, such as Austin down 21% and Chicago up 13.6% (ApartmentList, to June 2026). (row 1324)
  • Sales volume against the long-term average, for example Seattle down 29% (September 2026). (row 1801)
  • National price declines in Canada and New Zealand. (row 1339)

Partly supportedMorgan Stanley estimates the AI data-center build-out needs about $1.5 trillion of outside financing by 2028, with private credit supplying a large share.
Why

The core figure is right. A Morgan Stanley research note dated 16 July 2025 is titled "Bridging a $1.5tr Data Center Financing Gap" S72. It forecasts about $2.9 trillion of global data-center spending through 2028. It says roughly $1.5 trillion of that must come from outside the hyperscalers' own cash flow S72. Morgan Stanley strategists repeated the $1.5 trillion gap on their podcast on 6 August 2025 S73. One video (row 1371) says private credit would supply "$1 billion" of the gap. That is wrong: the note sizes private credit at about $800 billion S72. The rest comes mainly from investment-grade bonds (about $200 billion) and securitised debt such as data-center ABS and CMBS (about $150 billion) S72. Row 2215's line about "pulling $1.5 trillion out of debt markets" and competing with US Treasury refinancing is the presenter's own framing, not Morgan Stanley's. Row 3112's link to a $40 billion SpaceX raise is also the channel's own addition. The 2025 note does not mention it.

Contrary view: Morgan Stanley itself said it does not expect a financing bottleneck, arguing credit markets can absorb the issuance without strain [1].		Submitted directly, Tom Bilyeu, Upside Invest(rows 1371, 2215, 3112)2026-10-15S72 S73
SupportedDean Baker, Gita Gopinath and Oliver Wyman have each estimated that an AI-driven market correction would wipe out tens of trillions of dollars of wealth ($40 trillion, $20 trillion plus $15 trillion abroad, and $33 trillion respectively).
Why

All three figures match what their sources said. Dean Baker of CEPR wrote in June 2026 that US stocks are worth close to $80 trillion. If price-to-earnings ratios fell back to their long-run average of just under 20, that would destroy close to $40 trillion of stock wealth, "an average of almost $300,000 per household" S74. Gita Gopinath wrote in The Economist in October 2025 that a dot-com-style crash could wipe out over $20 trillion of American household wealth. She added that foreign investors could lose more than $15 trillion, about 20% of the rest of the world's GDP S75. She was IMF chief economist from 2019 to 2022 (the videos spell her name "Gopnath"). In January 2026 Oliver Wyman estimated that a crash like the early-2000s one would erase about $33 trillion of equity value at current valuations, "more than US GDP" S76. All three are scenarios, not forecasts.

Contrary view: These are conditional what-if figures; Oliver Wyman also set out a milder scenario in which air leaks out of AI valuations without a broad market collapse [3].		Patrick Boyle, Tom Bilyeu(rows 1805, 2185)2026-10-15S74 S75 S76
SupportedBloomberg analysis attributes about 40% of Germany's GDP shortfall to the energy shock, 40% to lost export markets and 20% to weak domestic demand and bureaucracy; separately, Bloomberg sees the copper market swinging into a deficit of about a million tonnes after a roughly 40% one-year price rise.

The Germany split is accurate. A May 2026 Centre for European Reform paper by Sander Tordoir and Brad Setser cites Bloomberg analysis from late 2024 S77. It says roughly 40% of Germany's GDP shortfall comes from lost export markets and 40% from higher energy prices. The remaining 20% comes from weak domestic demand, bureaucracy and other factors S77. The underlying piece is a Bloomberg Intelligence note by Martin Ademmer and Jamie Rush, "How 5 per cent of GDP got lost", dated 13 December 2024 S77. We could not read it directly. The copper claim (row 2281, 20 September 2026) also holds. BloombergNEF has projected a swing of nearly one million tonnes into deficit for 2026 S78. Other forecasters are lower: J.P. Morgan about 330,000 tonnes and ING 600,000 tonnes S78. Copper hit records in September 2026. One report put its gain over the past year at more than 46%, a bit above the video's "about 40%" S79.

Contrary view: Goldman Sachs has forecast a 300,000-tonne copper surplus rather than a deficit for 2026, so the million-tonne figure is the top of the forecast range [2].		Felix & Friends, Patrick Boyle(rows 1812, 2281)2026-10-15S77 S78 S79
SupportedAccording to the National Association of Realtors' annual survey, the median age of US first-time home buyers has risen to 40.

NAR's 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers was released on 4 November 2025. It put the median first-time buyer age at 40, a record high S80. The figure was 38 in 2024 S81. The survey covers purchases from July 2024 to June 2025. First-time buyers made up just 21% of buyers, also a record low. Repeat buyers had a median age of 62 S80. Both videos (July 2026) cite the latest NAR report correctly, including the November release. Whether this proves housing is unaffordable for young people is the presenters' reading. NAR does link the trend to high rents and debt. But the headline age is disputed. The Mortgage Bankers Association pointed to National Mortgage Database records. They show the median first-time buyer age went from 30 in 2014 to 33 in 2024, then dipped to 32 in 2025 S81. NAR's survey had a response rate of about 3.5% S81.

SupportedHarvard's Jason Furman calculated that AI-related investment accounted for roughly 90% of US economic growth in the first half of 2025.
Why

Furman posted on X in late September 2025. He wrote that investment in information-processing equipment and software is 4% of GDP but was "responsible for 92% of GDP growth" in the first half of 2025 S82. Without those categories, GDP grew at just a 0.1% annual rate S82S83. So "roughly 90%" is a fair rounding. Two caveats apply. First, the category covers all IT equipment and software, not only AI data centers. Second, it is an accounting share, not a counterfactual. Furman himself said that without the AI boom, lower interest rates and electricity prices might have made up about half the growth elsewhere S83. Row 1805 also mentions "more conservative estimates" of around 25%. We could not find that figure. Morgan Stanley's Lisa Shalett put data-center spending's boost at roughly 1 percentage point of real GDP growth S83.

Contrary view: Furman noted his 92% is not a counterfactual: absent the AI boom, lower rates and power prices could have offset about half of its contribution [2].		Patrick Boyle, Tom Bilyeu(rows 1805, 2185)2026-10-15S82 S83
SupportedA Wall Street Journal analysis found big tech firms carry about $3 trillion of AI-related commitments (unstarted leases and purchase commitments) disclosed only in filing footnotes, roughly five times their ~$600 billion of reported capex.

The Wall Street Journal published this analysis on 17 August 2026 S84S85. It reviewed footnotes in the latest filings of nine firms: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Nvidia, Broadcom, SpaceX and AMD. It found about $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments, mostly tied to AI S84S85. Roughly $1.2 trillion was leases that had not yet started, and $1.9 trillion was purchase commitments for chips, construction and energy S84S85. These sit outside the balance sheet because a liability is only booked once a lease starts or goods are delivered S85. Capex was about $600 billion, so the commitments were roughly five times larger S84S85. One detail is off. The $600 billion was capex over the past year, not one quarter, as the row 1805 wording says S85. Alphabet alone listed $811 billion of commitments as of 30 June S85. We could not open the WSJ original. These figures come from outlets that reported on it.

Contrary view: Much of the total is in normal contracts that are already disclosed in footnotes, and Morgan Stanley's accounting analysts called it hard to gauge, not hidden (as quoted in reporting on the WSJ analysis).		Patrick Boyle, Tom Bilyeu(rows 1805, 2185)2026-10-15S84 S85

Partly supportedThe IMF estimates that internal EU barriers, blamed on EU paperwork, cost firms the equivalent of a 44% tariff on goods and a 110% tariff on services.
Why

The numbers are real IMF figures. The goods figure is for manufacturing, and the cause is overstated. In its October 2024 Regional Economic Outlook for Europe, the IMF estimated trade barriers inside the Single Market. They equal a 44% ad-valorem tariff for manufacturing and 110% for services, against about 15% between US states S101. But the IMF does not say this is EU-imposed paperwork. It points to fragmented markets and national obstacles to the free flow of goods and services S101. The figures come from a gravity model. It compares cross-border trade with trade inside each country, and treats the whole gap as an "equivalent tariff". That gap also includes distance, language, home bias and where people live. Critics call these upper bounds, not a measure of red tape S102. Many of the services barriers are national rules, not Brussels rules S103.

Contrary view: Economists such as Max Görlitz argue the gravity-model gap mostly reflects language, distance and consumer preference, so reading it as a policy tariff badly overstates what regulation reform could achieve.		Patrick Boyle(rows 1819)2026-10-15S101 S102 S103
Partly supportedSeveral Federal Reserve banks estimate that break-even payroll growth has roughly halved since early 2024, meaning the labour market is tighter than headline job numbers suggest.
Why

Fed research does show break-even job growth falling sharply. But "roughly halved" understates the drop. The Dallas Fed estimates it peaked near 250,000 jobs a month in 2023. It fell to about 10,000 by July 2025 and averaged about -3,000 from August to December 2025 S104. A Federal Reserve Board note puts it at 155,000 in 2023-24 and 85,000 in 2025. It could fall below 10,000 a month in 2026 S105. The St. Louis Fed gives 153,000 in April 2025 and a 15,000-87,000 range for 2026 S106. So several Fed bodies agree on the direction, and most show far more than a halving. The "tighter than headlines suggest" reading is fair: weak payroll gains can still hold unemployment steady. The Dallas Fed found payroll growth from December 2025 to February 2026 slightly above break-even S104. The main driver is lower immigration, plus an ageing workforce S104S105.

Contrary view: Estimates vary widely with immigration assumptions (the St. Louis Fed's 2026 range spans 15,000 to 87,000), so a low break-even may signal weak labour supply and slower potential growth rather than a genuinely tight market.		Patrick Boyle(rows 1821)2026-10-15S104 S105 S106
SupportedNew York Fed research found Americans bore 94% of the 2025 tariff cost from January to August, falling to 86% by November.
Why

This matches the New York Fed's Liberty Street Economics post of 12 February 2026, by Amiti, Flanagan, Heise and Weinstein S107. It found that 94% of tariff incidence fell on the US side from January to August 2025. Foreign exporters absorbed 6% S107. The US share fell to 92% in September-October and 86% in November S107. Over 2025 as a whole, the authors say nearly 90% of the burden fell on US firms and consumers S107. Strictly, the research measures pass-through to US import prices. That burden falls on US importers first. It does not show how much was then passed on to consumers rather than absorbed in importers' margins.

Contrary view: The Trump administration publicly disputed the study's conclusions, and the import-price method cannot say how the US share is split between consumers and importing firms.		Patrick Boyle(rows 1830)2026-10-15S107 S108

The figures match Fed data, but the period given is wrong. The Fed's H.4.1 release tracks marketable Treasury securities held in custody for foreign official and international accounts. On Wednesday 8 July 2026 that stood at $2,597.3 billion S123. Its recent peak was $2,943.5 billion on 23 April 2025 S124. The fall between those dates is exactly $346.2 billion. From $2,800.6 billion on 11 February 2026, the fall is about $203.4 billion, close to the $203.7 billion cited S124. So the drop ran from April 2025 to July 2026, not 'mid-2024 to July 2025'. In fact, holdings barely changed between mid-2024 and July 2025, at about $2.93 trillion versus $2.88-2.91 trillion S124. The figures also cover Treasuries only. Agency securities fell separately, to about $208 billion S123. 'Reserve assets' is loose wording for what these numbers measure.

Contrary view: Custody holdings at the New York Fed are only part of foreign official holdings of US assets. SupportedUS M2 money supply has reached about $23 trillion and is growing at its fastest pace since 2022, with nearly $1 trillion added so far this year versus about $600 billion over the same stretch last year.
Why

The figures match Federal Reserve data. M2 was $23.34 trillion in August 2026, seasonally adjusted S145. That was the latest month published when the video went up on 30 September. M2 rose $987 billion from December 2025 to August 2026 S145. Over the same months of 2025 it rose $605 billion S145. So "nearly $1 trillion" versus "$600 billion" is a fair like-for-like comparison. For all of 2025 the gain was larger, at $868 billion S145. The growth-rate claim also holds. M2 was up 5.7% on a year earlier in August 2026, by our calculation from that series S145. That is the fastest annual growth since June 2022, when it was 5.7% and falling S145. Growth had turned negative from December 2022 to February 2024 S145. One wording point: the video calls the increase money "printed". M2 is mostly bank deposits, so its growth reflects bank lending and deposit flows as well as Fed actions. That framing is the presenter's own.

Contrary view: Measured over full calendar years, M2 grew $868 billion in 2025, well above the $600 billion the video gives for "last year" [1].		Felix & Friends(rows 2893)2026-10-16S145
SupportedThe Federal Reserve now expects inflation to stay above its 2% target until 2029 and has named AI investment as a force keeping prices elevated.
Why

Both parts match Fed documents. The FOMC's September 2026 projections put median PCE inflation at 3.7% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028 S146. The median first reaches 2.0% in 2029 S146. Core PCE follows the same path, at 2.2% in 2028 and 2.0% in 2029 S146. In June 2026 the 2028 median was 2.0%, so the target date slipped a year S146. The minutes of the 15–16 September meeting were released on 7 October, a day before the video S147. Fed staff projected inflation would "reach 2 percent in 2029" S147. They expected the effects of tariffs, geopolitical events and "the AI buildout" to wane S147. Staff partly blamed higher prices for technology-related consumer goods on the AI buildout S147. Some officials said it could push demand above supply over the medium term S147. Two nuances apply. The projections are medians of officials' views, not a single Fed forecast. The minutes list AI alongside tariffs and energy costs; AI is one cause among several, not the main one.

Contrary view: The projection materials themselves do not mention AI; the AI link comes only from the meeting minutes, where tariffs and energy costs are cited first [1][2].		Upside Invest(rows 3113)2026-10-16S146 S147
Partly supportedJ.P. Morgan forecast copper at $12,500 by the second quarter of 2026 and estimated that data centers could add about 500,000 tons of copper demand this year, a fivefold rise in global demand.
Why

The price target is real, but the unit is per metric ton. In December 2025, J.P. Morgan forecast LME copper at $12,500 per ton in the second quarter of 2026 S148. It expected a 2026 average near $12,075 S148. One video (row 2289) says "$12,500 per pound". That is wrong by a factor of about 2,200. By that video's date (2 May 2026), the forecast was also out of date. On 24 April J.P. Morgan put the Q2 2026 forecast at $13,500 per ton S149. Actual prices beat the older target. The IMF benchmark averaged $12,891 per ton in April, $13,512 in May and $13,552 in June 2026 S150. The demand figure is roughly right. J.P. Morgan estimated data-center copper demand at about 475,000 metric tons in 2026 S151. That is an increase of about 110,000 tons on the year S151. The "5x increase in global copper demand" is wrong. Global demand is about 28 million tons a year, so data centers are under 2% of it S151.

Contrary view: Row 2317 (8 March 2026) stated the $12,500 target when it was still J.P. Morgan's published view, with no unit error [1].		Felix & Friends(rows 2289, 2317)2026-10-16S148 S149 S150 S151
Partly supportedAt least 12 tankers were hit around the Strait of Hormuz in the week to 5 October 2026, the most since the Iran war began in February, and Goldman Sachs has modeled oil at $150 a barrel or more.
Why

The tanker count is right. Reuters reported at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers around the strait from 28 September to 5 October S152. Maritime security sources called it the highest weekly total since the war began on 28 February S152. The UN's IMO counted nine, a lower figure S152. The Goldman claims overstate the bank's view. In March 2026 Goldman's base case put Brent at $115 in April, falling to $80 by the fourth quarter S153. Its adverse case peaked at $140, and a "severely adverse" case peaked at $160 S153. So $150–160 was a tail scenario, not the forecast. Row 2267 (June) frames it as a conditional risk, which is fair. Row 2271 (21 September) says Goldman is "modeling" $150–160 for this year. That does not match Goldman's note of 8 September. It raised its December 2026 forecast by $5, and its upside case was Brent above $120 S154S155. Brent did rise sharply. It closed at $135.51 on 2 October S156. WTI averaged $97 in September S157. Neither has reached $150.

Contrary view: Goldman did publish a $160 peak scenario in March 2026, and Brent's October high of about $136 is closer to it than to Goldman's base case [2][5].		Felix & Friends, Peak Prosperity(rows 2267, 2271, 3316)2026-10-16S152 S153 S154 S155 S156 S157
Partly supportedUS Treasury yields reached their highest level in over 20 years, at 5.44%, while federal debt grew from about $7 trillion in 2004 to $40 trillion.
Why

The "highest in over 20 years" part holds for long-dated Treasuries. The 30-year yield closed at 5.59% on 29 September 2026, the upload date S158. The last close that high was in mid-May 2004, when it hit 5.61% S158. That is about 22 years. The 5.44% figure does not match any maturity on the upload date. On 29 September the 10-year was 5.26%, the 20-year 5.64% and the 30-year 5.59% S158S159S160. The video does not say which maturity it means. 5.44% fits the week before: the 20-year closed at 5.45% on 23 September, and the 30-year at 5.47% on 24 September S158S159. The 10-year never reached 5.44% in this run; its peak close was 5.31% on 5 October S160. Yields kept rising after the video. The 30-year peaked at 5.67% on 7 October, then fell to 5.43% by 15 October S158. The debt figures are right. Total public debt outstanding was $6.98 trillion on 2 January 2004 S161. It was $40.10 trillion on 29 September 2026, having crossed $40 trillion in August S161S162.

Contrary view: If the speaker meant the benchmark 10-year note, the figure is wrong: it closed at 5.26% on the upload date and never exceeded 5.31% [3].		ITM Trading(rows 3253)2026-10-16S158 S159 S160 S161 S162
Partly supportedThe Federal Reserve reported that US manufacturing output fell 0.3% in August 2026 against an expected 0.3% gain, with automakers saying strong sales would not last.
Why

The headline numbers are right. The Fed's G.17 release of 18 September 2026 said manufacturing output decreased 0.3% in August S163. It was the first fall after seven straight monthly gains S163. Durable goods output fell 0.5%, with broad-based declines S163. Trading Economics put the market forecast at a 0.3% rise, so "unexpectedly" is fair S165. First Trust put auto production down 1.2% in August S166. Note that First Trust's 0.3% consensus referred to total industrial production, which was unchanged S166. The automaker part is not supported. The Fed release says nothing about automakers' sales expectations S163. We found no source quoting automakers saying strong sales would not last. So that line, attributed to the Federal Reserve in the video, could not be verified. Later data softened the drop. The Fed's 16 October release revised August manufacturing to -0.2% S164. FRED's current IPMAN series also shows about -0.25% for August S167.

Contrary view: The core figure matches the Fed's first estimate exactly [1], so a reader could rate the claim Supported if the unverified automaker remark is treated as colour.		Eurodollar University(rows 2384)2026-10-16S163 S164 S165 S166 S167
ContradictedA Federal Reserve survey found that 40% of Americans could not raise $400 in an emergency.
Why

The source is the Fed's Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED). It does not ask whether people could raise $400. It asks how they would pay a hypothetical $400 emergency expense S168. In the latest survey, fielded in October 2025 and published 13 May 2026, 63% said they would pay with cash or its equivalent S168S169. That means cash, savings or a credit card paid off at the next statement S168. The other 37% mostly said they would pay another way, such as carrying a credit card balance or borrowing from family S168. Only 12% of adults said they could not pay the expense by any means S168. That was down from 13% in 2024 S168. So the video's 40% describes people who would not use cash, not people who could not pay. The 40% figure is also dated. The cash-or-equivalent share was 59% in 2017 and 61% in 2018, leaving roughly 40% S170. It has been 63% in each year from 2022 to 2025 S170.

Contrary view: The share who would not cover the expense with cash or its equivalent was 37% in 2025, close to the video's 40% [1].		Submitted directly(rows 2864)2026-10-16S168 S169 S170
Partly supportedThe Fed's preferred inflation measure, PCE, stood at 2.4% for the year before the Iran war and was revised upward after the conflict began.
Why

The 2.4% figure is real, but it was a forecast, not measured inflation. In December 2025, Fed officials' median projection put 2026 PCE inflation at 2.4% S171. At their 18 March 2026 meeting, they raised that projection to 2.7% S172. Press reports tied the upgrade to higher energy prices from the war in Iran S173. So the video is right that the Fed's figure was revised up after the war began. But actual PCE inflation was never 2.4% in this period. The latest data before the 6 April upload came out on 13 March 2026. It showed PCE prices up 2.8% from a year earlier in January, and core PCE up 3.1% S174. February data, released after the upload, again showed 2.8% headline and 3.0% core S175. Current BEA data on FRED put headline PCE inflation at 2.7% to 2.8% from October 2025 to February 2026 S176. It then rose to 3.4% in March and peaked at 3.8% in May 2026 S176. Core PCE stood at about 3.0% to 3.2% through mid-2026 S177. The video does not say the 2.4% was a projection, so viewers could mistake it for actual inflation.

Contrary view: If the video meant the Fed's own year-ahead projection, the claim is accurate: the median 2026 PCE forecast did rise from 2.4% to 2.7% in March 2026 [1][2].		Felix & Friends(rows 2304)2026-10-16S171 S172 S173 S174 S175 S176 S177

Why

The broad trend holds, but several specific figures do not. The World Gold Council (WGC) says central banks bought 1,136 tonnes in 2022, the most on its records back to 1950 S178. Buying stayed above 1,000 tonnes in 2023 and 2024 S179. The 2010–2021 average was 473 tonnes a year S179. So row 2227's "most this century" holds. Its "fastest since 1997" does not match the WGC data, which put the record further back. Row 2230 says banks "now" buy over 1,000 tonnes a year. That was out of date by September 2026: 2025 buying fell to 863 tonnes S179. Its "one-third of production" is also high. Mine output was a record 3,672 tonnes in 2025 S180, so even 1,000 tonnes is about 27%. Row 2204 has three errors. China's central bank bought no gold in May 2024, ending an 18-month streak S181. The record first quarter was Q1 2024, at 290 tonnes S182. Q1 2026 was first put at 244 tonnes, not a record S183. WGC later cut that estimate to 57 tonnes S184. Q2 2025 was also below 200 tonnes, at 166 S185. Row 2228's "$22 billion in three weeks" could not be checked. The WGC publishes central-bank demand quarterly, not weekly. Q2 2026 rebounded to 289 tonnes, a record for a second quarter S184.

Contrary view: Buying of 289 tonnes in Q2 2026 set a record for a second quarter [7], so the pace may be picking up again. The 2022–2024 buying was the strongest on WGC records back to 1950 [1][2]. Method & limits

Which videos

700 videos are in scope: Felix & Friends 114, RE-V 112, Upside Invest 112, Eurodollar University 74, Tom Bilyeu 56, The Timeless Investor 52, Submitted directly 51, ITM Trading 49, Patrick Boyle 43, Peak Prosperity 37. RE-V videos carry over from the housing roundup. Named channels were kept on an economic keyword score, with borderline videos reviewed by hand. Videos the reader sent in directly were kept on a keyword score or a yes/no check of their published summary by a small model, with borderline cases reviewed by hand. Richard Taylor's wholesaling videos and Will Barron's sales videos are left out.

Dates

The date is the video's upload date (665 videos). Where none was found, the date the video was transcribed is used instead (35 videos); those months may be shifted. Backfills mean some channels have many old videos and others only recent ones.

Stance scores

A small model read each video and scored its outlook on seven topics, from −2 to +2, or left a topic blank if the video did not discuss it. For RE-V videos the score was made from the existing summary card. Scores are a rough reading, not a measurement. Each channel counts equally per month; videos sent in directly count as one channel. On average the channel-weighted figure differs from the per-video average by 0.14 points.

Strength test

The time view leads only if a topic has at least 3 months with 15 or more scored videos, and its monthly line moves by more than the typical spread within a month.

Fact-checks

The most-cited attributed claims were checked against primary sources where possible. Housing claims checked for the RE-V roundup are reused with their original check date. A figure seen only in search results or a secondary report is marked †. No URL is made up.

Trade ideas

The trade ideas are this report's own analysis, not a channel's view. They are built in four steps. (1) A signal ledger is built in code: card points grouped into thirteen cross-market transmission nodes (for example housing volume, homebuilders, mortgage credit, private credit, AI capital spending, the curve), with channel stance, theme heat, fact-check track record by channel, the most repeated channel recommendations, and live prices for about ninety instruments. (2) A model reads the ledger, not the transcripts, and proposes twenty candidate ideas, each a causal chain that cites its rows. (3) Each candidate is checked by a separate reviewer against live prices, valuations, option chains and official data: does the cited evidence say what the idea claims, and has the market already moved? (4) A second reviewer argues against each survivor. The ideas shown are the ones that survived both. Option prices are mid-quotes from the chain on the stated date and will have moved. Conviction is a judgement, not a probability.

What this is not

This is not investment advice. Channel opinions are reported as claims by their authors; the trade ideas are analysis for information only.
